The AI Incident Database, currently containing 271 incidents with $55%$, $31%$, and $14%$ originating from technology, healthcare, and transportation sectors respectively, is presented in this paper. Our analysis of the database involves exploring characteristics of incidents, such as their causes and consequences, and examining how various stakeholders are involved in these events. The AI Incident Database is made available for public use to foster a collective understanding of AI system failures and promote more resilient AI technologies.

The principle underlying the renormalization group is that the behavior of large
objects can be predicted from the rules governing the interactions of their
component parts. Although this approach provides valuable insights in statistical
mechanics and quantum field theory, puttin it into practice is challenging. A new
algorithm known as the gradient flow is offering a novel means to implement the
renormalization group at the level of experimental measurements. In terms of
renormalization, this approach remains within the self-contained paradigm, a
conceptual framework in which an object is described by removing interactions one
at a time. However, the gradient flow has been shown to be equivalent to an
integration technique called the continuous renormalization group. A new
interpretation of the gradient flow is presented here, one that transforms this
technique into a numerical method capable of solving differential equations with
non-constant coefficients. This approach can be applied to a wide range of problems
involving boundary problems, equations with fractional derivatives, and keta-function
equations, along with their applications in quantum field theory and probability
theories.

This paper investigates methods for checking consistency between evolving models and real-world observations of business processes. We draw a distinction between two types of discrepancies that can arise: (i) discrepancies which can be resolved by adjusting either the process model or the observations, and (ii) discrepancies that cannot be resolved as the process model and the observations are inherently incompatible. We propose a method to identify and address type (i) discrepancies by generating a set of possible solutions, while type (ii) discrepancies remain unresolved and are highlighted through the creation of incompatible automata.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to two process modeling languages: (1) workflow models with regards to the semantic properties related to soundness and (2) models with obstacles, in relation to the semantic properties related to termination, where the process model and the observations are equivalent if the process is free from obstacles. The benefits of this work lie in its ability to provide a mechanistic approach for identifying and resolving inconsistencies between process models and real-world observations, highlighting its practical applications in the domains of business process re-engineering, process governance, and performance measurements.

Quipper, a quantum circuit description language, makes compiling quantum algorithms into executable code feasible. The stability of quantum algorithms within varied noise environments depends heavily on the precise implementation details, which can differ based on the particular hardware being used. The proto-Quipper extension in this research introduces a type of abstract semantics that generates a universal, general machine code applicable to any quantum hardware. The addition of flow control, recursive functions, and variable storage in proto-Quipper-M enables the compilation of quantum algorithms into hardware-independent code that is also executable on quantum simulators. The resulting ccode is shown to be capable of accurately tracing the runtime state of quantum programs, and its compilation to quantum hardware is compatible with the Quipper language used in actual hardware.

In this study, we have modelled a two-dimensional field theory that involves complex statistical problems, specifically dealing with the dynamics and behavior of random matrices above and below their critical point. Above this point, these matrices exhibit smooth, predictable scaling properties; whereas below it, their behavior is characterized by sudden, extreme changes. Through numerical analysis based on the Lanczos algorithm and by utilising the properties of equidistant node distributions, we have explored the properties of these matrices and developed relationships between their above- and below-critical- point behaviors. Our findings reveal that, despite their differing natures, these behaviors exhibit a connection that allows us to predict and explain the occurrences of the extreme changes. This discovery provides a framework for understanding and identifying the critical point and the patterns of the extreme changes. Additionally, our results show that above the critical point there is agreement with established theories, particularly in relation to the patterns of the extreme changes. Our work and these findings were originally presented at the Les Houches Summer School in July 2019.

We suggest developing a quantum sensor using a collection of $^{148}\textrm{Nd^-$}$ dipoles, isolated in an optical cavity, for making precise measurements of optical phase. A series of laser pulses will be used to create pairs of dipoles in a squeezed state, and then interact with the cavity. The sensor will be designed to operate over long periods, due to the long-lived ground state of the dipoles, with the capability of detecting very small changes in optical phase, and thus detecting weak interactions between the dipoles. It is anticipated that this sensor will be able to make accurate measurements of optical phase at the level of $10^{-4}$ rad, and even detect weak non-linear interactions between particles, providing significant insight into many-body physics.

Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to create continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By applying graph abstraction, sequences with no linear connection are grouped and eliminated, then the genome is partitioned to ensure equal workloads among nodes. Through reassignment and subgraph computation, sequences are optimally distributed across nodes. Finally, sequences within each partition are merged to form the complete genome, demonstrating up to 67 times speedup on 128 cores over a naive approach.

A well-established logistic model has been expanded upon, leading to the introduction of a new delayed logistic equation. This new model is based on the ordinary logistic growth law but incorporates a delay that forms a non-linear interaction term. The global dynamics of this equation are investigated by first transforming the discrete time version into a fractional order system, which is then analyzed in the context of the theory of Caputo fractional derivatives. The study reveals that the global dynamics of the delayed logistic equation reduce to those of the ordinary logistic model under certain conditions. The outcome also holds true for other delayed logistic equations, confirming its universality. The global dynamics of the delayed logistic equation are influenced by the delay parameter and the global dynamics of the ordinary logistic model, making them highly dependent on these two factors.

The concept of statistical depth has the potential to be used extensively for measuring the hierarchical ranking of both multivariate and functional data within temporal frameworks, however, it remains largely unexplored in the field of temporal point process research. We propose a new depth measure, called the Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation, that enables the extension of established point process models to simultaneously account for data hierarchies and the temporal rankings of events. These models can then be used for estimating both the model parameters and the temporal rankings of events. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the ILR approach through the application of it to various practical problems, such as detecting periods of high activity in a neurosignal and tracing the evolution of a subpopulation of cells in a brain signal. We also verify the efficiency of the proposed method via both simulations and the analysis of an additional dataset related to a subpopulation of cells in a brain signal.

Superconducting metamaterial machines have the potential to offer more efficient and powerful options for optimizing energy transfer between magnets, which could lead to a significant reduction in civil aircraft weight and associated environmental emissions.
The optimal performance of these metamaterial machines is heavily dependent on the field patterns and the arrangement of the superconducting strips, as well as their spatial spacing.
This study investigates an idealized superconducting hybrid machine consisting of combined flying-rib and flying-tip configurations in a Helmholtz coil setup, driven by a simple strip design.
The analysis focuses on the coil's omnidirectional coupling to the strip, and an analytical formula derived in this research is used to determine the optimal spacing between strips for maximum coil efficiency.
The results show that an ideal hybrid machine can achieve a significant resonant frequency enhancement, and the device's coil efficiency can be significantly improved, yielding an enhanced figure of merit (FOM) 10 to 100 times greater than that of conventional flying-rib technology.

Researchers employed proton-induced reactions on enriched targets to produce exotic isotopes of germanium. By detecting the excitation functions of various transfer reactions, specifically those involving the $^{22}$Ne($^{16}$O,$^{18}$O)$^{24}_{10}$Ge* de-excitation channel, they successfully produced 12 previously unmeasured states within germanium isotopes. Specifically, 7 new states and 5 significantly updated states were discovered around the N = 40 region. Utilizing the collective information gathered from $\beta$-delayed $\alpha$ particle emission and other decay modes, researchers were able to study the properties of these newly explored regions of germanium isotopes. Notably, around N = 40, nuclear structure properties exhibit an abrupt shift from deformed to quasi-spherical structures. Additionally, around the single-particle shell closing point N = 40, nuclear shell transitions are found to be strongly influenced. Further analysis revealed that nuclear shell transitions in the A = 70 region are characterized by a complex mixture of proton and neutron shell transitions.

Researchers have introduced an innovative technique for accurately measuring the masses of extremely short-lived, unusual atomic isotopes over a wide range of frequencies. This method utilizes the principle of isochronous mass spectrometry, leveraging the instantaneous detection of ions at the point of resonance to eliminate the need for lengthy cycles. Incorporating simulation-based candidate selection and targeted experiments, the team has successfully measured the masses of two exceptionally short-lived isotopes, $^{46}$Cu and $^{50}$Cu, with exceptional precision. These groundbreaking measurements will significantly impact our understanding of nuclear physics and enable more precise analyses in nuclear medicine and high-precision geology.

In contemporary lattice field theory, standardization is an approach being developed to eradicate statistical ambiguity in simulated data, a concern that becomes particularly pronounced with the rise of more intricate theories and larger system sizes. The general strategy involves deconvolving the integrals that define observables with the help of Green functions, which are determined through lattice simulations. The lattice community is currently at an early stage of implementation, with the majority of advancements centered on the application to momentum-space observations. This invitation to participate presents an overview of the concept, focusing particularly on the underlying principles and the challenges that remain to be addressed, in the hope of gathering contributions that address the technical details of this challenging problem.

We aim to improve the accuracy of structured text recognition by incorporating predefined patterns derived from expert knowledge, expressed in a straightforward and flexible format using regular expressions. Our approach is initially confined to a limited set of features but can be easily expanded to support various features without requiring fundamental modifications. The intensity of the biasing effect can be adjusted according to the confidence levels of the initial predictions. The accuracy of our method is validated on a range of structured text datasets, including addresses, dates, and product information, and compared to a baseline model with a more complex form of biasing.

The cross section measurements of top quarks produced in proton-proton collisions are often at the forefront of quantifying dependences of hadronic particle production on the properties of the parton that initiated the interaction, particularly when those partons come from heavy quarks due to their distinctive Q dependence. Although direct measurements of top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions are not feasible yet, due to the low availability of these events, it is crucial to understand how top quarks would be detected in such collisions to interpret results from the Large Hadron Collider with reliable theoretical accuracy. To achieve this, I present calculations of the detection cross sections of top quark pairs in proton-nucleus collisions, utilizing next-to-leading order QCD results, by accounting for the effects of parton radiative corrections and incorporating different schemes for how parton showers are handled, including a virtual parton approximation for when the parton is not directly detected. I will also discuss how these results are extended to detect not only top quark pairs but also the production of top quarks in association with a W boson, considering different possible detection outcomes, including when hadronic quarks produced in the interaction are not detected, which requires the use of next-to-leading order QCD results even for parts of the proton that do not interact with the nucleus, in order to accurately account for the effects of perturbative QCD corrections.

This research addresses the text-to-SQL semantic interpretation challenge in the vertical language understanding category, focusing on translating natural language input into SQL queries based on database content. We investigate the cross-domain implementation of this translation, which involves considering various databases and their corresponding contents. The project consists of two components: first, identifying the relevant database to use for a given text, and second, converting the text into an SQL query based on that database's content. We develop a two-stage model incorporating attention and auxiliary tasks for database selection, and a follow-up SQL generation module using a stack-based model with attention. We test different approaches and present our findings, achieving notable performance improvements over existing benchmarks in the end-to-end evaluation setting. Notably, our results show a 10% absolute gain in MORDAC scores across multiple benchmarks, and a 16% absolute gain in MORDAC scores when applying a pre-trained language model to our approach.

The ongoing LoTSS survey is conducting a thorough observation of the Northern sky to better understand how the large-scale structure of the Universe changes and develops. Although only 1% of the sky is being intensely mapped, initial findings have already given scientists new insights. Researchers used the first data release of LoTSS, mapping 1.3 square degrees with 150 MHz band data, to study galaxies and their relationship to large-scale structures. Employing sophisticated analysis tools and taking into account various sources of error and uncertainty, researchers discovered that at large distances of up to 250 Mpc, galaxy power spectrum follows expected linear patterns. However, at shorter distances, there are non-linear patterns that could be linked to complex structure morphology, or possibly be the result of data contamination. Additionally, investigating the relationship between galaxies and radio sources, researchers found that early galaxy formation types are more likely to be associated with active galactic nuclei. Using galaxy size and color as indicators, researchers classified over 100,000 galaxies in the observed area, with nearly all galaxies classified displaying linear patterns on large scales. Furthermore, regardless of color, galaxies tend to be more densely packed in smaller areas than massive elliptical galaxies. By combining data from LoTSS and the nearby UDS-cosmology project, researchers estimated that galaxies that are brighter than a certain threshold are associated with a bias of around 2.6 times more than less bright galaxies. These findings, obtained from 150 MHz data, align with previous

This paper introduces an advanced adaptive-sieving algorithm designed to tackle the High-Dimensional Rank Lasso problem, a crucial regression analysis challenge. To handle the vast number of potential features in high-dimensional scenarios, our approach employs a comprehensive generalization of the sieving strategy, incorporating both variable selection and rank-ordered penalty terms. Our adaptive-sieving approach is then combined with a customized interior-point method to yield an efficient and highly effective algorithm. Extensive numerical testing, utilizing synthetic and real-world data sets, firmly establishes the robustness and performance capabilities of our proposed algorithm. Furthermore, our analysis confirms that this algorithm offers a significant enhancement in computational efficiency when compared to its closest competitor, SPG-RL. With remarkable results across various data sets, our adaptive-sieving algorithm has proven to be an excellent addition to the collection of efficient algorithms already available in the research literature for solving the Rank Lasso problem.

We examine the thermal response of a two-level system both statically and dynamically using convex entropy production principles. In both cases, the entropy generated per cycle is quantified and found to be minimizable with specific optimal conditions, thereby maximizing the system's cycling efficiency. Notably, this methodical approach to minimizing entropy production achieves faster and weaker driving forces than previously possible methods. Additionally, this technique of reducing entropy production promotes the development of multiple metastable states, thereby increasing the likelihood of achieving stable cycling.

The beneficial influence of AI on environmental issues is widely acknowledged, yet its overall effect when implementing these solutions necessitates a deeper examination. We advocate for a more accurate assessment of AI-based environmental initiatives, highlighting the hidden consequences associated with certain actions, good intentions, and the common method of double-bottom-line approaches, which frequently depend on the premise that reducing the cost of one resource will automatically lead to a gain for another. Conversely, AI-driven environmental rectification may sometimes result in net losses, necessitating innovative resolution mechanisms to address these complexities.

This paper explores the current state of business process monitoring by examining prescriptive intervention techniques that use predictive models to address issues at the next step in a process execution. Our analysis reveals a notable gap in research on prescriptive process monitoring, particularly when it comes to using predictive models for proactive decision-making purposes. To address this discrepancy, we propose future research directions in predictive process mining, such as automatically detecting predictive models from historical data and incorporating prescriptive process monitoring capabilities into real-time business process management systems.

A posteriori error estimation is addressed for a Boussinesq model of fluid-heat interaction that generalizes the traditional approach by allowing temperature-dependent density and heat transfer coefficients. Two multigoal-oriented error estimation strategies are developed and applied to solve a benchmark problem, and the techniques demonstrate acceptable accuracy for the given mesh resolution.

Cependant, lorsque des conditions de consistance sont impliquées, ces problèmes deviennent NP-complètes, ce qui rend difficile leur résolution en temps raisonnable. Malheureusement, à ma connaissance, aucune méthode d'homogénéisation n'a été proposée pour les problèmes de pilement de barres avec contraintes. This paper explores a model of confidence that is linked to a dynamic preference model, specifically the balance theory. We show that in a situation with multiple triangles of opposing opinions, only one stable state exists, in contrast to a situation with one inverted triangle and multiple opposing outward pointers, which has multiple stable states. We demonstrate that these models share characteristics with other research, such as "plausible denial" and "strategic ambiguity", and like the diffusion of behavioral changes, they too exhibit two different types of transitions, slow and rapid.

We've found a detailed description of a asymptotically flat black hole with hair, consisting of three components: a core, a mesosphere, and an atmosphere. The core, where the gravitational force is extremely strong, has a uniform density and is described by a series of harmonic oscillators. The mass of the black hole can be compared to that of a guitar string, with specific notes. The frequency of these notes, known as the Tonality, becomes higher as the mass of the black hole increases. The mesosphere, situated between the core and the atmosphere, acts as a resonator that amplifies the sound produced by the harmonic oscillations. The atmosphere, which extends to the point where the density of the black hole is infinite, consists of a series of waves that describe the state of the system in its momentum space. The wave function of the atmosphere, called the Densitaly, contains all the information needed to determine the appearance of the dark star. The boundary between the mesosphere and the atmosphere is called the Densitaly node, and is located at a distance that varies depending on the mass of the black hole, and is greater than the size of the core. The behavior of the system, and therefore its Densitaly, is determined by the fundamental quasimodes of the system. Different genes exhibiting similar levels of activation may still display distinct patterns of RNA synthesis, implying varying production rates or delays. However, current methods for analyzing transcription data are primarily designed for genes with uniform RNA production rates, which makes them unsuitable for comparative studies. A new model called the Delay-Rate Model has been developed to quantify and compare the RNA production rates of individual genes across different species or cell types. This model enhances traditional approaches and provides more accurate estimates of RNA production delays, both above and below a threshold of 30 minutes. Using Delay-Rate Model analyses, the correlation between RNA production delays and coding versus non-coding regions of long non-coding genes has been examined, and the findings suggest that these genes exhibit shorter RNA production delays if they are closer to protein-coding regions. Furthermore, the Delay-Rate Model enables the identification of transcription units within non-coding genomes by treating them as a collection of genes with uniform RNA production rates, and the model's capabilities have been validated by comparing RNA production rates in wild-type and Drosophila melanogaster mutants for which chromatin structure is known.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes.

In recent years, researchers have made significant progress in supersymmetric dual theories, a concept introduced by Seiberg. Without supersymmetry, this field faces more difficulties, but exceptional models offer hope for finding general principles behind non-supersymmetric dualities. We're concentrating on three highly speculative models - the SO(4) vector theory, the SU(2) fundamental theory, and the SU(3) fundamental theory - all lacking supersymmetry. These theories are thought to have highly complex dual models, but exceptional examples could shed light on general duality practices.

A linear complementary pair of group codes $(C, D)$ is formed when the direct sum of $C$ and $D$ results in the entire group algebra $R[G]$, given a finite commutative ring $R$ and a finite abelian group $G$. We are specifically investigating this phenomenon in the context of primary ideal rings and providing a full characterization of linear complementary pairs of group codes in this scenario.

We present a novel, compact, and efficient functional parameterisation that, when used within an integer programming framework, yields a straightforward solution to the MAP problem in graphical models. This novel approach simplifies the integer programming formulation, eliminating the need for variable dispatching and directed edge indexing variables, thus reducing the size of the LP relaxation and time complexity to a practical O(n^3) level. Our proposed method also offers a straightforward means to resolve constrained optimisation problems. Experimental results demonstrate that the new framework surpasses existing state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of runtime, while remaining highly effective in solving the constrained optimisation problem.

The rapid growth in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) technology has led to a surge in applications, but ensuring safety in human-UAV interactions has raised concerns. To address this issue, we have developed a novel system called FlyHelp, designed to detect fallen items on UAV paths and provide real-time warnings to users. This innovative system effectively integrates asynchronous audio and visual data to accurately locate the fallen item's position, allowing for easy installation on UAVs without additional equipment. After collecting and processing visual and audio data, the system utilizes the detected audio signal's characteristics to identify the item's location, and the image data is used for confirmation. Experiments conducted in open spaces yielded a precise object localization rate of 85.72%, with a processing speed of less than 150ms.

We perform a comprehensive review of shear thickening transitions in various systems, including colloidal suspensions, granular materials, soft materials, and traffic flow. Our analysis reveals power-law viscoelastic scaling relationships in all of these areas, and we provide a unified explanation for the observed scaling behaviors through a simple model. We also discuss the implications of our study for theoretical research in shear thickening phenomena.

This study undertakes an exploratory analysis of daily electricity consumption patterns in Ghana's capital city, focusing on understanding the hourly dynamics of energy use. We find notable seasonal variations in electricity usage, largely attributed to temperature, which is in turn influenced by humidity. Notably, there's a strong correlation between electricity consumption and temperature, with users attempting to mitigate the effects of the power crisis by adjusting their energy usage in response. We also uncover a range of hourly patterns in electricity usage, which can be effectively represented using the TGOSTM distribution. We begin by examining the general characteristics of electricity consumption patterns, including the derivation of the cumulative distribution function, before progressing to the analysis of daily patterns. We utilize the knowledge that electricity usage patterns are repeatable on a daily basis to construct a daily time series model, which incorporates temperature and humidity as key predictor variables. We leverage the TGOSTM distribution to model the hourly components of electricity usage, highlighting the practical benefits of this approach for forecasting purposes. We also demonstrate how our daily model can be adapted for forecasting purposes, while providing recommendations for practical applications of our findings.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the extent to which these biases may influence their work. The data collected reveal that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms while their work relies heavily on Google's Web search. This study also highlights the range of potential biases that can occur in search algorithms and the extent to which these biases may lead to the omission of crucial information that is relevant to the participants' professional work. In total, the participants may be omitting as much as 19% of relevant information due to their reliance on Google's Web search. This study stresses the need for increased transparency and accountability in Google's Web search algorithms to prevent the omission of relevant information.

Understanding natural language APIs through visual programs can be facilitated by interpreting flow charts, but the diverse range of elements within these charts poses a significant challenge for generalization. To address this issue, we developed the Graph Recognition Convolutional Neural Network (GRCNN), a model that extracts modulated program features by recognizing graph elements. By employing a customized attention mechanism and a parameter-sharing strategy during convolution, GRCNN enhances program generation performance and produces a notable improvement of 6.1% in accuracy compared to the existing convolutional neural network (CNN) approach. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the proposed framework yields a notable improvement of 7.6% in program generation performance compared to a method that utilizes visual program guides with modulated attention.

This text explores various reduction techniques employed in climate science 
for modeling complex systems. It begins with a examination of the intricacies 
in climate modeling at various scales, before delving into prominent methodological 
solutions such as dynamical, model-order reduction, and energy-based reduction 
techniques. Each reduction method is dissected, along with examples of its 
application in climate modeling and analysis. Ultimately, the report highlights 
future avenues for research, emphasizing the need for more comprehensive 
evaluation of reduction algorithms in climate science.

Recent discoveries of gravitational wave events have made it possible to study kilonovae closely, and understanding their properties relies heavily on accurate opacities, energy distribution, and other atomic data. Our paper provides the most comprehensive tables of energy levels, radiative rates, and energy distribution for the Os isoelectronic sequence, including Os, Ir, Pt, Au IV, and Hg II. We also outline our approach to constructing the Os isoelectronic sequence model, and include a special focus on gold, which is a critical element in kilonovae ejecta. Our gold model is particularly significant due to its role in defining the spectrum in the near-IR and UV regions. Our final tables are tailored to meet the needs of researchers in astrophysics who require precise atomic data to study kilonovae effectively.

The gallbladder's ideal location for sonographic assessment is often obscured by excessive fat deposition in the upper right abdominal area. Such cases necessitate a clear visual distinction between the gallbladder and surrounding visceral organs, especially the right lobe of the liver and the pancreas. The region of interest near the gallbladder needs to be segmented accurately for further evaluation, but this can be challenging due to the presence of adipose tissue in the area. In this research, a novel approach based on deep learning and RethNet architecture is presented to automatically segment the gallbladder and its surrounding visceral organs from abdominal ultrasound images, without the need for manual adjustment. The performance of the proposed model was evaluated using the SIIM-ACR PR-Net Challenge data, and the results showed its efficacy in handling different types of lesions and imaging modalities while accounting for the variations in organ location due to factors like disease and the absence of a standard reference shape.

Compositional data analyze relationships within systems composed of multiple interconnected components. The calculations and visualizations used in these data are distinct from standard statistical methods. This tutorial explains the unique mathematical approaches, provides examples of the specialized visualizations, and offers guidance on the correct interpretation of the results in the context of compositional data.

The hypothesis that massive sub-Saturn exoplanets are rare within the sample of planets discovered through the CORALIE/HARPS radial-velocity survey has been supported by previous researchers. This theory was based on the finding that sub-Saturn masses were often close to the brown dwarf boundary, suggesting the possibility of planetary or boundary case exceptions. However, the main objective of our study was to investigate the completeness of the CORALIE/HARPS sample in terms of detecting planets near the brown dwarf boundary and to derive a theoretical distribution of the planet mass ratio, p(Ms; all). Another goal was to investigate the frequency of the planet mass ratio, p(Ms; <3 R_J), in the CORALIE/HARPS sample, comparing it to the predicted frequency from the Core Accretion Simulated Planetary Populations model (CASPP). 

We analyzed the relationship between the signal-to-noise ratio and the semi-major axis of the planets in the CORALIE/HARPS sample and discovered that the boundaries for radial-velocity detectability are at a 0.325 AU radius for hot Jupiters and a 4.5 AU radius for longer-period planets with masses greater than 4 Earth masses. Furthermore, our study found that the point of non-detection for the warm sub-Jupiters is at a 1.3 AU radius.

In intelligent systems with multiple sensors and actuators, a controller must efficiently use available resources to achieve optimal performance by actively selecting which sensor signals to gather from the environment and process. Our approach involves training a resource-aware controller to maximize the correlation between its chosen sensor data and its output actions, using a mutual information maximization method. This method allows the controller to prioritize relevant sensor information, reducing noise and redundancy, and has been proven to converge reliably. Additionally, we have shown that our approach can be applied to a variety of controllers, including neural network controllers, under both offline and real-time conditions. The results of our experiments confirm that our method successfully enables the controller to actively collect relevant sensor data, resulting in more efficient operation with limited resources.

To explore the lower mass spectrum of dark matter that can be compressed, we have chosen a model where a dark matter particle $\chi$ is linked to other fermions $\psi$ through a Yukawa interaction, resulting in a non-relativistic, contact-like interaction that becomes significant at lower dark matter velocities. Within the framework of heavy Yukawa theory, we've calculated the Yukawa coupling $Y$ in terms of the dark matter mass $M$, the new fermion mass $m$, and the dark momentum $p$. In a specific realization where the new fermion is the lightest state, we've established relationships between these variables that influence the Yukawa coupling. We've further analyzed, using a simplified annihilation model, how this interaction affects the dark matter density fluctuations in various velocity regimes, ultimately influencing the current dark matter density. We've discovered that for certain values of $M$ and $m$, the compressed dark matter with a Yukawa interaction can be stable on an astrophysical time scale and may contribute significantly to the total dark matter density.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can learn to perform complex tasks such as predicting the next word in a sentence or navigating a complex environment by generalizing from a limited number of experiences.
Even simple RNN models can excel at these tasks when presented with ample data and the structure to succeed, achieving faster training times than competing methods.
In numerous cognitive tasks, an RNN's weights can be set randomly and still enable efficient learning, potentially due to the inherent structure of the task data.
We propose an evaluation framework that assesses an RNN's potential by simulating various cognitive tasks and observe that a fixed-sparse RNN can learn many of them quickly.
Our results indicate that the hybrid RNN architecture, specifically the one with the inter-dependent leaky integral (ILI) component, performs well across several task types by generalized information exchange within its internal structures, thereby requiring fewer complex weight mappings.

We introduce a mathematical framework to classify different types of nilpotent algebras based on their underlying mathematical structures. Specifically, we develop a method to categorize these algebras based on the properties of their ideals, which are constructed from a nilpotent basis of the algebra's underlying vector space. The quality and relationships between these ideals serve as the key indicators for the algebra's type. We demonstrate that the set of isomorphism classes among nilpotent algebras can be equipped with a structure of a topological space, where the categories of nilpotent algebras with a specific number of dimensions, and those that are finitely generated in those dimensions, form a continuous spectrum. We establish a mathematical representation for the algebra's decomposition that depends on the properties of its ideals, and provide a method to compute this representation for any given nilpotent algebra. We also study the limits of the algebra decomposition as the number of dimensions approaches infinity.

In the early universe, large radio galaxies like 8C1908+47 and J2152-4209 had jets that must have been powered by supermassive black holes at incredible distances of over 13 and 13.4 billion light-years, respectively. It's thought that radiation from the cosmic microwave background could have had a significant impact on these jets, particularly as they emerged from their galaxies and expanded into the surrounding environment. This has led to a proposal that radiation from the CMB could have had a significant impact on the evolution of black holes and their jets, especially during the early universe. This could lead to a shortage of powerful radio galaxies at the highest redshifts. Here, a model of jet expansion is presented, taking into account the pressure of the expanding jet and its interaction with its environment, as well as the effect of radiation from the CMB. This model is applied to the simulation of radio galaxies in the early universe. It's found that radiation from the CMB can reduce the maximum distance that jets can travel and affect the shape of radio galaxy distributions, particularly at the highest redshifts. This could also influence the rates of black hole growth and the energy output of relativistic jets, especially as they travel longer distances.

The current research in metric-affine gravity theory involves modifying Einstein's general relativity by allowing a non-metric, dynamic torsion field within the theory's framework. Torsion is not only allowed but also considered a fundamental aspect of gravity's geometric structure. In order to assess the viability of metric-affine gravity, researchers have raised the question of whether a Lagrangian that incorporates a non-vanishing torsion field is variational. In other words, they have asked if the action principle can be applied to the theory when the torsion field's equation is derived variationally. In our study, we examine the covariant derivative of the Einstein-Hilbert Lagrangian in relation to torsion, and we consider alternative Lagrangians that combine a gravitational field with torsion. We have determined that the Einstein-Hilbert term is invariant under any torsion field, and we have calculated the canonical Hessian matrix for the combined Lagrangian, determining its stability in the process. In our analysis, we assume that the torsion field's form can be expressed in terms of a geometric, coordinate-independent fashion. Additionally, we have derived the field equations resulting from varying the action principle with respect to both the metric and the torsion field, and we have discussed the implications of these findings in the context of geometric structure and physical observability.

This study presents an enhanced approach to 3D image features that incorporates invariance to discrete symmetry by considering inversions of spatial axes and image contrast.  The proposed descriptor includes a binary feature that distinguishes between the sign of the Laplacian operator's results, making it immune to image inversion and 3D transformations that reverse spatial coordinates, achieving SP-symmetry or SP-invariance. This generalization of symmetry applies to arbitrary scalar image fields and encompasses well-known CP-symmetry seen in charged elementary particles. Local feature orientation is represented as the gradient direction related to the sign of the Laplacian, which determines the feature direction. Two novel results relate to computing the gradient direction and combining it with the sign of the Laplacian: (1) the gradient direction can be represented by projecting the signal's gradient magnitude in the direction of the signal itself, and (2) the combination results in a descriptor that is invariant to image inversion and 3D spatial transformations, achieving SP-symmetry. This approach is demonstrated using the publicly available CPD dataset of cerebral blood vessels, where registered points, and partially aligned vessel structures, are effectively obtained under SP-invariant conditions. This research is the first to achieve registered points, and partially aligned vessel structures, under SP-invariant conditions.
