We successfully completed the winning solution to the 2022 NeurIPS MRL Challenge by addressing the practical issue of physical simulation not accurately matching real-world images. We approached this problem by utilizing image gradient statistics, which are simple to create in both simulated and real-world settings, to bridge the simulation-to-reality gap. We developed an open-source dataset, called the 'gradient dataset,' comprising a vast collection of image gradient maps from both simulated and real-world images. This gradient dataset serves as the foundation for our challenging task of integrating automatic driving into a simulated environment. We applied a straightforward yet effective method to create the gradient dataset by applying a Laplacian of Gaussian filter to both simulated images and real-world images. We then trained an encoder model to produce a compact representation of the gradient data, which we subsequently use as a basis for comparing and matching simulated and real-world data. Notably, our method bypasses the need for real-world data during training, allowing for greater flexibility. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by achieving a high track completion rate and maintaining a low collision rate in real-world tests. The source code for our challenge solution has been made publicly available at: https://github.com/sony/sony_mrl_nips_2022_neurips_challenge

Deepfake creation techniques continue to evolve at a rapid pace, allowing for the production of high-quality videos with minimal visual discrepancies. Despite the existing differences, it's plausible that future deepfake detection methods will struggle with unidentified, specially crafted and adversarially crafted samples. To address this challenge, we have developed an advanced deepfake detection model that utilizes a self-sustaining neural network design, combining XLU data and adversarial samples to achieve better performance. Our research showcases the effectiveness of this approach, with the neural network achieving impressive results on various datasets, notably MFAD, FAD, and FMD. This method demonstrates superior performance compared to other leading competitors on the same datasets, with notable improvements of 5.41%, 3.13%, and 2.13% respectively. Furthermore, we have found that using XLU data in deepfake detection provides a significant enhancement in performance, with an average improvement rate of 9.06%. This research not only addresses the issue of deepfake detection discrepancies on various datasets but also offers a reliable method for improving models on unclassified data sets.

The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's is a significant breakthrough in the search for life beyond our solar system. To better understand these planets' internal compositions, we focused on the interactions between their solid cores, H/He gases, and H2O oceans. We developed a new approach, distinguishing between the effects of gas solubility and the thermal relationships between the gas and the liquid. This distinction allowed us to determine the mass of a sub-Neptune exoplanet (K2-18 b) based on its observed transit spectrum. We found that our model, taking into account gas solubility, yielded a more accurate internal temperature profile and a smaller core radius. Notably, the solubility model enabled us to determine the mass of a sub-Neptune exoplanet that is typically hidden by its atmosphere, and our results for K2-18 b suggest a core radius of less than 1.3 times that of Earth. Our model also implies that a H2O ocean is necessary to explain the observed transit spectrum of this planet. Our findings demonstrate that the relationships between an atmosphere and an ocean within a sub-Neptune exoplanet can be better understood through their transit spectra by differentiating between the effects of solubility and thermal relationships.

Inspired by the continuous-time learning process in living organisms, a new paradigm has been developed for learning in spiking neural networks. The existing difference-based learning algorithms are modified and adapted for use with analogous time-based learning mechanisms. However, these modified algorithms are impractical due to their data dependence and computationally inefficient. To overcome these limitations, a novel, biologically feasible spike-based learning algorithm, called Backpropagation Through Time, has been proposed and tested in a simple robotic task. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this new algorithm in reducing the stability issues associated with the original Backpropagation Through Time, and its feasibility in real-world spike-based neural networks makes it an attractive alternative to existing deep learning methods.

This paper explores the impact of out-of-category examples on models trained with supervised learning, revealing that they frequently result in incorrect predictions and misinterpretations of data. It examines the current state of research in dealing with out-of-category instances and highlights the shortcomings of models that have not been adapted to handle such instances. Utilizing the transformation of ImageNet from a within-category to an out-of-category task by removing category labels, researchers discovered that superised models often perform poorly and that self-supervised models, which have not encountered similar data, achieve better results. Images from the new dataset, named Out-of-Category ImageNet, can be accessed on the https://twitter.com/VincentFraigne platform.

A specific approach, known as Generalized Polynomial Chaos expansion, is used to approximate random functional dependencies, which can be validated through two main methods: one is an analytical method that evaluates the error and confirms convergence, and the other, more commonly employed, relies on a post-evaluation method that estimates the error but doesn't confirm convergence. This study focuses on the post-evaluation approach and introduces a novel technique for measuring errors in GPU-Chaos expansions, which are often used in high-dimensional problems. In addition, this method enables assessing the convergence of GPU-Chaos expansions, allowing for assessing the accuracy of approximate values and confirming or refuting the convergence of chaotic expansions. Several numerical case studies are conducted to highlight the proposed approach and demonstrate its capabilities.

To address the limitations of existing change detection methods that assume complete data availability, we have developed a framework for detecting and isolating changes in partially observed sequential systems. Our approach incorporates an adaptive procedure using empirical Bernoulli approximations to build a statistical model, which is based on a Markov chain and can accommodate various types of data disruptions. By focusing on the detectability of a change and minimizing false positives, our model avoids the bias towards changes that affect a majority of the system's states. It is also capable of handling arbitrary models and data patterns without prespecifying a model class. In addition, by leveraging the statistical power of the normalized statistics and the continuity of the state transition function, we have established a condition that ensures our method's consistency. Experimental results across various domains, including online learning, network monitoring, and system identification, have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach in detecting changes under partial data observability and outperforming existing change detection methods.

We have obtained high-resolution spectra of nine dwarf galaxy globular clusters, which were obtained using the Very Large Telescope's UV-Vis Spectrograph. This new research enhances the existing database of iron, sodium, magnesium, aluminum, silicon, calcium, titanium, and nitrogen readings in these ancient cluster stars. Analysis of the newly acquired data indicates that the smallest dwarf galaxies in our sample, such as Leo I and Leo V, are composed of cluster populations with similar ages and chemical makeup as more massive galaxies like the Milky Way. However, the more massive dwarf galaxies in our sample, such as Scullin 1 and Dragonfly 404-1, have both younger and older cluster populations. If these clusters continue on their current paths, they will soon merge with the main galaxy. We have discovered that the chemical composition in the smaller dwarf galaxies is similar to the chemical composition in the bigger ones, but the chemical composition varies significantly across different galaxy types. This new research is the first to compare iron, sodium, and other element readings between the core clusters of a bigger galaxy and its smaller satellite galaxies, and it shows that the chemical composition in the smaller dwarf galaxies is similar to the chemical composition in the bigger ones, but the chemical composition varies significantly across different galaxy types.

We establish that the mapping spectrum $M\mathscr{A}$ of a profinite group $\mathscr{A}$ carries a natural action by $\mathscr{A}$, whose associated fixed-point spectrum is denoted by $M\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{A}$. A homotopy-type theorem states that the spectrum $M\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{A}$ can be homotopy-equivalent to the spectrum obtained from taking the direct product $\hat{\mathbb{Z}}\times \mathscr{A}$ after ignoring the basepoint at $(1,0)$. This result generalizes the work by Klucki-Mislin-Mislin-Ranicki, who previously found that the spectrum $M\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{A}$ can be homotopy-equivalent to the spectrum $M\mathscr{B}$, where $\mathscr{A}$ acts on the profinite group $\mathscr{B}$ via a homomorphism. Additionally, we show that if $\mathscr{A}$ acts trigonally on a finite CW-complex $X$, then the action extends naturally to a trigonal action of the profinite group $\hat{\mathbb{Z}}\times \mathscr{A}$ on the CW-complex $X\times (0,1)$.

The efficiency of optical character recognition in extracting data from documents is heavily dependent on the quality of its labeled data. However, obtaining precise manual labels for a large dataset can be extremely costly. This article presents a new approach called "semi-self-supervised OCR", which significantly reduces data labeling costs by combining a small set of high-quality labels with auto-labeled data using the trained model itself. The experiment demonstrates that a relatively small set of $|D_{\text{hi}}|$ high-quality labels can effectively extract useful information from a much larger dataset of $|D_{\text{lo}}|$ low-quality labels, even when the initial labels are inaccurate. As a result, semi-self-supervised models require only a tiny fraction of the data labeling costs associated with fully supervised models. The code for this approach can be accessed at https://github.com/dyrobson/document-extraction.

The interface electronic structures of InAs/EuS and EuS/InAs heterojunctions have been studied using a coordinate scaling method, accounting for the significant difference in lattice constants between the two materials. Our findings reveal that the interface energy bands of InAs/EuS pivots around the (100) plane, whereas those of EuS/InAs pivot around the (011) plane. Our calculations also show that the effective mass of the interface states differs significantly between the two configurations, with the mass of the EuS/InAs interface states being nearly five times larger than that of the InAs/EuS interface states. Our study is the first to theoretically examine the electronic structures of EuS/InAs heterojunctions, and our results provide a foundational understanding of the materials' properties essential for developing spin-transistor applications.

A fundamental concept in continuous logic encompasses spaces $X$ with a topology derived from a metric $\rho$, where the topology becomes Borel when employing the Wadge metric. This research delves into simplifying the hierarchy of Borel Wadge classes by reducing the infinite hierarchy to a finite one, thereby making the classification system more manageable. To achieve this, we build upon Cohen's forcing technique to demonstrate that for any infinite level $\alpha$ of the hierarchy, the next level is equivalent to a specific collection of subsets known as meager sets. This insight, in turn, allows us to identify the highest level of the hierarchy as $\omega_1$ and enables efficient classification of Borel Wadge classes. That efficiency comes from being able to compute the $\sup$ of Borel Wadge degrees of subsets of any space $X$ with a topology derived from a metric $\rho$, where the topology becomes Borel when employing the Wadge metric. This research also yields an infinite hierarchy for a specific collection of subsets called analytic sets, where the highest level of the hierarchy is $\omega_1$ for any space $X$.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are increasingly being adopted for a range of tasks, such as image classification, object detection, and segmentation. However, the immense size of their models leads to slow inference speeds on mobile devices and high computational requirements during training. Previous studies on model pruning have focused on removing entire convolutional layers or groups of layers, which inevitably alters the original model architecture and compromises accuracy. There has been little research on fine-grained pruning of CNNs at the individual convolutional layer level. Our work introduces ClickTrain, an efficient and precise end-to-end deep learning training technique that leverages fine-grained pruning of CNNs. ClickTrain pioneered a novel architecture-preserving pruning approach focused on the most critical convolutional layers in state-of-the-art models, allowing for substantial reductions in model size without sacrificing accuracy. ClickTrain then optimizes the pruned models using a combination of accelerated training techniques, such as LayerNet and PolyNet, which enable fast and precise model training. ClickTrain successfully prunes models on the ImageNet, COCO, and Cityscapes datasets to meet specific hardware constraints toiling, thereby facilitating swift and precise deployments of high-quality CNN models on mobile devices and in the cloud. The project's code is available at https://github.com/zyh420/CliCKTrain.

This research examines the addition of three modal operators ($\Diamond$, $\Box$, and @) to the Distributive Complete Lambek Calculus, maintaining their validity in the process. We address the resulting logical system's soundness, its relationship to modal sequences, and the properties of its modal axioms within this context. We demonstrate that the system's modal operators can be interpreted through a semantic framework incorporating labelled modal sequences and its associated Kripke semantics. By substituting sequences for single labels, we can model the operators $\Diamond$ and $\Box$, while the @ operator is represented by a structural duality. We find that the system's modal operators $\Diamond$ and $\Box$ do not adhere to the traditional modal axiom patterns. We explore the operator @'s relationship to duality and its implications on the system's modal architecture, examining its properties and potential catamorphic duality in the process.

The detections of binary compact objects, specifically black hole - neutron star mergers, have provided valuable opportunities to understand the late stages of stellar evolution and the behavior of dense objects. Their gravitational waves, spanning multiple frequency ranges, need to be analyzed by both theory and machine learning algorithms to identify their source types. A deep learning approach is able to identify whether a signal is from a black hole - black hole or neutron star - black hole merger, and the model is able to handle real-time data analysis. A notable result is that the deep learning model's accuracy in identifying neutron star - black hole mergers is significantly higher than the previously established likelihood-based method. Furthermore, we find that neutron star - black hole mergers have an estimated event rate of 25 events per year at 250 Mpc distance. Future upgrades to the LIGO, Virgo, and other gravitational wave detectors will greatly increase the number of detections, enabling more precise studies of dense objects.

A fascinating new discovery has been made on the exoplanet TOI-5542 d, a gas giant with a mass similar to that of Jupiter. Researchers have determined that this planet orbits a 1.07 solar mass star approximately 430 light-years away, completing one revolution in just under seven days. Using a detailed analysis of the transit data and other data types, such as the brightness variations and the relative movement between the planet and the star, the team has gained valuable insights into the properties of the planet. One key aspect that caught their attention is the planet's relatively large size, which is on the cusp of being classified as a hot Jupiter. Additionally, the discovery revealed that TOI-5542 d is now navigating a wider orbit as a result of experiencing significant internal heat. Further investigation into the properties of the planet and its surroundings is ongoing.

This research develops a primal-dual method for solving constrained Markov decision processes, offering a practical solution that can be easily implemented and providing a quantifiable error estimate. The approach adapts the primal-dual stochastic gradient, a common method for constrained optimization, to solve the constrained Markov decision process. The resulting algorithm is shown to converge at a rate of O(1/t) with t iterations, and is accompanied by an efficient primal algorithm that converges at a rate of O(1/sqrt(t)). The method is evaluated using a grid-world problem and compares favorably with existing methods in terms of computational efficiency.

This research targets the recognition of mathematical handwritten notes using an offline approach, focusing on the analysis of system architecture rather than specific algorithms. The study introduces a novel dataset consisting of 80,000 mathematical text examples spanning both basic and advanced topics across four languages, dubbed the "MathDataset". This dataset is crucial not only for evaluating mathematical handwriting recognition but also for enhancing mathematics education and research. The math recognition system is an intricate challenge due to diverse mathematical symbols and algebraic structures. Our work presents an advanced architecture that distinguishes and generates multiple mathematical text segments, leveraging the MathDataset and effective training methods to achieve high accuracy levels in recognition.

We establish connections between superconformal quantum mechanics and superfield theories in four dimensions by examining the growth of cohomology spaces of specific sheaf types on non-singular Grassmannians. In superconformal quantum mechanics, we find that non-trivial cohomology occurs in odd degrees, leading to infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. In super Yang-Mills theory, we identify similar infinite-dimensional spaces through the study of differential forms and cohomology on Grassmannian spaces. Our analysis also implies the existence of diverse spectral triads associated with superconformal field theories and Lie superalgebras. Notably, we demonstrate that simple super Yang-Mills theory features a spectral triad with a 7-dimensional base, a 14-dimensional middle, and a 21-dimensional top.

This study investigates the relationship between complex network properties and the unpredictability in their interconnected systems. We analyzed this by projecting a dataset of human social interactions onto two-dimensional space and observing the complex networks' evolution over time. Our results indicate that areas of high activity and high instability in the networks coincide, contrasting with areas of low activity and high stability. Furthermore, the study reveals that the onset of instability in the networks is preceded by similar patterns of activity increase, suggesting a threshold effect. It has also been found that the prevalence of these patterns rises as the networks approach instability. These findings provide insights into the unpredictability in complex interconnected systems and the potential for detecting impending system failures through variability analysis. The research may be applied to other complex systems such as electrical or transportation networks.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning has significant practical applications in areas such as robotics and we can see its usage in Model Predictive Control (MPC). However, its convergence relies heavily on the use of a linearly interpolating policy, which often results in a unstable and unpredictable iteration process. By incorporating Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) theory into actor-critic methods, we have developed a new technique, known as the Hamiltonian Policy-based Actor (HPA). Theoretical analysis has proven that the HPA algorithm converges at a rate of O(1/sqrt{T}) and has stable and smooth policy interpolations. Moreover, our experiments have demonstrated that the HPA method outperforms the traditional actor-critic algorithm and often achieves higher rewards, especially in difficult reinforcement learning tasks.

It's widely presumed that there are infinitely many prime twins, pairs of prime numbers that differ by a fixed, relatively small margin ($2$ in this case). We offer a straightforward proof of this assumption by leveraging a fundamental result that was initially demonstrated using analytical methods.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a difficult challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional navigation systems may struggle to operate effectively. To overcome these challenges, this research presents a novel indoor navigation system that utilizes a layered controller to combine data from sonar and vision systems, enabling reliable and real-time localization in unstructured environments. A key contribution of this work is the development of a vision-based assistant that employs a machine learning-powered association model to streamline the process of sonar image feature matching. By leveraging this approach, the system has demonstrated substantial performance enhancements, making it suitable for real-time application. Experimental results validate the efficiency and reliability of the proposed method, demonstrating its capability to operate in real-time and outperform a widely used feature-matching approach by matching more correlation pairs per frame.

NII Nereid, a satellite of Neptune, has been analyzed using data from the Wide-field Infrared Spectrometer (WIRPS) on board the Kepler spacecraft. We used this information to determine the spectral characteristics of NII Nereid by applying two different models. The first model revealed the presence of polar water ice that has been altered by the presence of other compounds, covering about 10-20% of its surface, as observed at temperatures below 253K. However, this model struggled to explain the observed strength of the 3.0$\mu$m water ice band. A second model incorporated more detailed assumptions about the composition and distribution of ice and rock on NII Nereid, as well as atmospheric factors, using data from two different observations. This model determined that the surface of NII Nereid is primarily composed of water ice that has been changed by the presence of other compounds, covering about 50-70% of its surface, as observed at temperatures between 253-263K. The model also indicated the presence of organic compounds, as well as other compounds such as ammonium chloride and magnesium chloride, as observed at temperatures between 253-263K. The spectra from NII Nereid are not consistent with a surface composed of pure water ice, as observed at temperatures between 253-263K. as well as other compounds such as ammonium chloride and magnesium chloride, as observed at temperatures between 253-263K. Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of order $n \geq 2$, consisting of elements from the finite field $F(q)$ of order $q \geq 2$. Furthermore, let $V_{2n}(q)$ be the free left module of its components of order $2$. In our work, we demonstrate that the left projective line over the ring $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ bears a unique isomorphism with the left projective line over the ring $L_{2n}(q)$. Moreover, we establish that the affine plane and the projective plane of order $q^n$ are isomorphic to the left affine plane and the projective plane of order $q^2$ respectively, both of which are based on the given ring $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$.

This study extends ordering with models, a method for evaluating mathematical theories, to include Tukey-order with models. We demonstrate that replacing the original's $R$-order with $R$ itself maintains continuity in this extended framework. We then examine fundamental properties and distinctiveness of four essential concepts in this framework, all of which were previously investigated in the original ordering with models. We also explore new ideas, such as the notion of distinctness of theories, and analyze how these properties relate to various models of infinite set. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between distinctness of theories and uncountability of models, before using specific examples to illustrate the potential non-equivalence of these properties.

A new method is introduced for improving a policy's effectiveness, specifically its ability to generate positive outcomes, using a model-based approach that leverages historical data. This approach, which is centered around a key performance metric called negativity, enables researchers to identify the most effective policies and quantify the benefits of alternative policies. To achieve this goal, a novel optimization technique is developed, combining Bayesian learning and mathematical programming to pinpoint optimal policies at both a general and customized level. To address the challenge of variability in policy evaluations, a Bayesian framework is used for modeling uncertainty, while the integration of performance metrics and policy assessments is handled by a dual transformation. Finally, a Bayesian version of the epsilon-support vector machine is used to classify policies based on their efficacy.

Dualities between category theory and other fields often facilitate the translation of homological concepts from one setting to another. This paper explores duality pairs consisting of a category, a type of preservative inclusion, and a subcategory of minimal objects that preserve this inclusion. It then demonstrates how such dualities can be utilized to translate various homological concepts between the categories involved. Specifically, the paper establishes that if a subcategory of minimal objects preserves a particular inclusion of functors, then certain minimal objects in both the category and the subcategory of minimal objects preserve this inclusion when restricted to a particular class of morphisms. This paper also examines the implications of this finding for dualities between Grothendieck categories and other homological concepts.

A proposed $E_8$ network in Higgs boson collisions is examined for non-Abelian quantum connections and the nonlocal properties of entanglement and contextuality. A model of eight coupled bosonic wires in three-dimensional space, similar to a quantum version of the $E_8$ graph, is studied. By quantizing a real field that is based on an $E_8$ lattice, a complex field definition is created, allowing for a dual version of the original system to be obtained, which exhibits distinct properties. In contrast to the original system, the dual system shows maximum contextuality and the maximum degree of entanglement possible for its given number of particles. Additionally, the dual system exhibits a number of discrete symmetry transformations, often found in spin systems, which may be verified experimentally.

A particular type of topological band structure, characterized by no edge states, can give rise to superconductivity when paired electrons interact with each other. We investigate this scenario for a specific two-dimensional superconducting system where the single-electron energy spectrum consists of smooth, curved bands. Employing a self-consistent approach, we analyze how the superconducting gap forms and find that its distribution varies significantly with the curvature of the bands. In direct contrast to earlier research on linearly dispersive topological bands, we observe multiple condensate wave vector(s) in the range of the Fermi surface. We further demonstrate that the superconducting gaps can be stabilized at low temperatures through the pairing of electrons. Additionally, we outline key experimental indicators that could help verify our predicted superconducting gap structure.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the distributions of a special type of combinatorial object, show that a certain function of a polynomial of these objects has a symmetric distribution, and prove this symmetry is unique. We then extend the proofs of two known theorems, obtaining more general results in the process. The first, an adaptation of the second of these theorems, has implications for the study of finite Ramsey sets. The second, an extension of the first, has implications for the study of finite sets.

In the analysis of high-dimensional data, such as microarray gene expression, presences-absences data are often collected to identify co-operating biological functions across multiple datasets. This analysis aims to cluster genes across multiple studies in order to determine overlapping biological functions. In this study, we assessed the performance of six clustering methods designed for high-dimensional data, as well as two alternative approaches, using simulated and real data. Our results show that these clustering methods can accurately recover synthetic datasets based on simulated data, but perform less well on real data, suggesting they may be useful for initial assessments of presences-absences data. However, due to their low accuracy, these clustering methods should not be used for definitive inferences about biological functions.

Current leading salient object detection models often discard valuable geometric information present in images, focusing solely on pixel-wise relationships. In contrast, previous studies that utilized 2D and 3D data in conjunction with existing models were limited by their reliance on external depth data from stereo or RGB-D images. To address this, our proposed framework captures image geometry in an efficient and accurate manner, enabling the development of novel and effective methods for salient object detection using RGB and RGB-D data. By leveraging a self-encoding mechanism and a novel graph-based fusion approach, our framework achieves superior performance, setting a new benchmark with a single model that surpasses 22 existing methods. Additionally, our framework allows for the creation of a data-driven method that exploits learned features from large image datasets, resulting in a significant performance boost of 8.2% in metric scores.

This paper presents our approach to the SemEval-2019 Task 6, which focused on detecting aggressive language toward a specific individual in social media posts. Our strategy involved two distinct models, both addressing different aspects of the problem. First, we utilized BERT, a pre-trained language model, to classify the overall sentiment of a tweet. Subsequently, we developed an SVM-based model to identify the content within a tweet that was targeted and aggressive in nature. Our final strategy combined the outputs of both models, along with additional features, to classify tweets as either directly or indirectly aggressive toward the specified individual. Our system demonstrated a macro-F1 score of 0.5243, achieving a macro-averaged F1 score on the test data.

A number, N, that can be expressed as the sum of the squares of m primes (where m is odd) is classified as palindromic; otherwise, it's not. We examine subsets of these classes resulting from dividing out numbers by a certain divisor, d. Additionally, we investigate and record findings on a related set of numbers, N/d, when d is not a perfect square.

We introduce a novel non-convex variational framework for CT reconstruction, noise reduction, and material decomposition in polyenergetic X-ray sources. Our formulation simultaneously translates these tasks into a complete system of first-order partial differential equations, which we solve using an iterative implicit scheme near a stable equilibrium point. Experimental reconstructions reveal a satisfactory balance between softening hard edges and minimizing noise, while our approach effectively differentiates between multiple material densities.

This research presents a novel approach to handwritten text recognition, specifically for languages with limited available data. Unlike traditional methods that require extensive labeling, our approach leverages the information contained in public datasets to train a single model for a specific language. By utilizing public datasets with annotated translations, we create a comprehensive training set for the target language, synthesizing it into a single document. This document can then be used to train a single model that can handle a range of complex languages, including those with vertical, cursive, and complex scripts. To validate our method, we successfully applied it to Modern Hebrew, which was shown to surpass the performance of a leading off-the-shelf HCR system, with results that compared favorably to a system specifically tailored for that language using labeled data from Israel's national dataset.

In a first, we combine different computational methods for forming a complete picture of heavy atomic nuclei. Specifically, we use a merged calculation that incorporates the results from three distinct approaches: a relativistic spherical single-nucleon model, a multi-configuration Gaussian-based method for calculating ground atomic states, and a relativistic cutoff model for describing excited states of heavy nuclei. We focus on the nuclei with atomic numbers ranging from 26 to 104 and demonstrate that the employed approach produces accurate results, particularly for the ground states, in line with recent experiments. Furthermore, our method is capable of accurately determining masses, half-lives, and 2-neutron separation energies, in agreement with experimental data on nuclei consisting of both light and heavy protons and neutrons. We also find that the employed approach is capable of accurately describing two-neutron and two-proton separation energies across the entire range of studied nuclei. In addition, we identify regions of stable nuclei against beta decay and find that our results are in good agreement with experimental data on the half-lives and energies released during this process.

This comprehensive review delves into one of the most influential models in condensed matter theory, the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, to uncover hidden symmetries within various topological phases. The article unfolds as a journey, starting with the initial decisions made in the development of the SSH model. Along the way, conceptually important interludes examine fundamental ideas related to topological properties, while a comprehensive mathematical foundation is established for understanding topological phases and phase transitions. The review then systematically analyzes multiple aspects of the SSH model, incorporating ideas from interband interactions, higher-band extensions, and other generalized models. Ultimately, the inclusion of lattice vibrations in topological phenomena is explored, but left unsolved in the reviewed models. The author expects that this review will serve as a foundational resource for those new to the topological phenomena associated with the SSH model, as well as a reflective overview for established researchers working on generalizations of topological phenomena.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. Furthermore, an analysis reveals a previously overlooked crossing symmetry in the preamplitude, which can be utilized to create a symmetric function that encodes all relevant information about the preamplitude. Through this approach, we are able to directly obtain the AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ supergravity amplitudes without requiring the deformed Wilsonian effective action recently introduced by Piskunov.

The accelerated computing paradigm on GPUs, enabled by the use of the CUDA programming model, offers superior performance. However, explicit memory management in CUDA can be a challenge, particularly when working with complex data structures, due to the risk of memory fragmentation and inefficient memory access. If left unoptimized, this can result in memory-related errors, including allocation failures, incorrect results, and program termination. In this research, we introduce a parallel memory allocator called DynaSOAr, designed to streamline memory management for object-based programming on GPUs. By utilizing a slab allocation approach, DynaSOAr eliminates the complexity of manual memory allocation, including header management, and provides a simple and efficient framework for real-world applications, as demonstrated by our results, which show a speedup of up to 2x and an improvement of up to 2.3x over the current implementation.

We introduce two high-scale $U(1)_{X}$ models derived from the SO(10) theory, 
addressing the anomalies in the Standard Model and explaining the origin of neutrino masses. 
The first model includes a $U(1)_{X}$ charge for the Higgs doublet, leading to 
a non-trivial Higgs vacuum expectation value impact on the $Z_{2}$ identity, 
potentially causing the little hierarchy problem. 
In contrast, the second model incorporates a $U(1)_{X}$ charge for the right-handed fermions, 
leading to a trivial Higgs vacuum effect. 
To maintain consistency with the SO(10)$\ni W_{P}$ anomaly-free condition, 
we choose a specific form for the additional $U(1)_{X}$ charge, necessitating 
an interpretation of the $Z_{2}$ identity. 
To compensate for the loss of SO(10) unification in the gauge couplings, 
we propose an extra $U(1)_{X}$-charged particle with a mass much higher than the GUT scale. 
Within the context of electroweak symmetry breaking, 
we evaluate the allowed mass ranges for the additional $U(1)_{X}$-charged states. 
Furthermore, under the assumption of minimal fine-tuning for electroweak symmetry breaking, 
we examine the potential impacts on the $Z_{h}$ mass and coupling strengths.

A comprehensive analysis of a cane tube under axial tension and internal pressure has been conducted. Assuming a perfectly fit tube with no slippage, we investigated how these forces impact the cane's stability. To determine the effects, we used Euler's elasticity theory to identify critical pressure levels for both the cane and the surrounding solid and semi-flexible can materials. Additionally, the consequences of premature failure due to excessive internal pressure have been taken into account, resulting in the development of an equation that relates tension to pressure and radius of the can. Furthermore, we considered a real-world scenario where the cane has slight lateral movement due to wear, calculating the resulting force equivalent in terms of the deformation and temperature conditions. To facilitate practical applications, we have provided users with two-designed charts to determine the can material type and conditions suitable for different canes.

In practical scenarios with limited and imperfect data, relying on classical probability theory can be overly conservative, prompting the development of methods that analyze networks under varying levels of uncertainty. We focus on maintaining the reliability of conclusions drawn from these networks, ensuring they remain robust against changes in parameter distribution parameters. Our approach transforms the uncertainty analysis into a semialgebraic geometric computation problem on the real projective space, providing an innovative framework for quantifying the reliability of these network conclusions with quantifier elimination techniques and probabilistic circuits. We illustrate the efficacy of this method by comparing it against alternative approaches, such as Monte Carlo simulations, in a real case study from healthcare.

In this research, we report Wannier-Stitzter states-based Bloch oscillations in ultrasonics, where we observed Wannier-Stitzter states in a 2D piezoelectric crystal and used a theoretical model to verify that the Wannier-Stitzter states can induce acoustic Wannier-Stitzter states. Our study reveals that the acoustic Wannier-Stitzter states can occur in any crystal that has an inversion symmetry, and we propose two methods to excite them experimentally.

In this study, we explore the interplay between neighbor-transitive codes, partial spreads, and the automorphism groups of generalized quadrangles. Initially, we establish a link between the codes and the quadrangles through an equivalent relationship. Subsequently, we demonstrate the existence of specific code arrangements - four-dimensional subcodes - within the graphs of these generalized quadrangles. These codes form the basis of partial spreads of certain projective spaces, and their properties are thoroughly examined. We also provide a comprehensive list of all possible linear codes in the graphs of quadrangles, and show that these codes possess a neighbor-transitive property when they are also non-trivial and have a certain code weight.

By utilizing color-invariant two-dimensional correlation functions applied to stellar counts from the Gaia mission's data release two, we determined the anisotropic density of the Central Molecular Zone to be approximately 2.4 x 10^5 LUpc^2, which aligns with the anisotropic density framework's predictions for this region. We note, however, that the Correlation Function Technique yields lower stellar density estimates compared to other methods. Additionally, we found the Gaia mission's EDR3 provided more accurate results than DR2, mainly due to improved stellar position precision.

To analyze changes in short-lived electronic structures on an atomic scale
following large doses of radiation, researchers use a specific type of quantum
measuring tool called the Resonance Enhanced X-ray Absorption Near edge Structure
(REXANS). They have created mathematical frameworks that describe how electronic
structures modify over time in response to radiation doses, and have applied
these models to simulate experiments for specific types of materials. For example,
they have used a model to simulate changes in the electronic structure of a
metallic material called nickel oxide as it transitions from a metallic state to
an insulating state at higher radiation doses. Furthermore, they have used
another model to examine how a different material, perovskite, modifies its
electronic structure as it transitions between different types of insulating and
conducting states. These simulations not only confirm a known phenomenon where
electrons tend to form groups at higher radiation doses, but also highlight how
these electronic groups exhibit non-linear patterns of excitation and de-excitation
at higher radiation doses. These findings suggest that there may be a critical
point beyond which materials can no longer absorb radiation in a linear fashion.

This research develops a temperature sensor chip utilizing a novel temperature-dependent current comparator, which is based on a PMOS transistor and exhibits current nonlinearity. To address this issue, the temperature sensor design incorporates a digital calibration module, enabling the conversion of the current comparator's nonlinearity into a precise temperature reading. The proposed temperature sensor design features a $ \pm$1.4{\deg}C error budget, 0.24{\deg}C resolution, and 81.4kb bitstore, with power consumption of 3.56uW from a 1uA to 100uA current range, and 1.06nJ per conversion energy at 1Hz sampling rate. The design's temperature coefficient error was reduced to $\pm$1.4{\deg}C through 16-bit binary calibration. The sensor chip was fabricated using SMIC's 0.18um CMOS process, with a 0.25mm$^2$ active chip area.

Quantum entanglement is a key feature of quantum physics that also holds the potential to outperform classical approaches for various applications, including enhanced sensing capabilities and improved communication efficiency. However, the process of generating and distinguishing entangled states is notoriously challenging. A heralded approach offers a solution by leveraging the trade-off between entanglement creation and differentiation, as it allows for the extraction of entanglement-based correlations upon detection of a signal indicating its generation. This goal is achieved in our experiment by employing a quantum scissors technique that can identify entanglement through direct measurement of a signal, thereby eliminating the need for complex differentiation procedures. By utilizing this Heralded approach, we have successfully created and demonstrated polarization-entangled photons with a high level of accuracy and quantifiable error margins.

This research paper explores the concept of digital Euclidean spanners - a type of geometric spanner created using digital (bitwise) metric computation. Building on the concept of digital metrics introduced in 2009, the paper delves into their application in geometric measurements. It presents a method for generating digital Euclidean spanners and demonstrates their potential for solving complex geometric problems. However, the paper also shows that digital Euclidean spanners lack the applications of traditional geometric spanners, since their underlying digital metrics do not adhere to the triangle inequality. Finally, the paper proposes the concept of short digital metrics, introducing the term 'β-skeleton' and outlining potential areas of investigation.

Accurate categorization of IoT devices is a critical requirement for safeguarding IoT systems from security threats and implementing data protection regulations.  The rapid growth in IoT corresponds to an explosion of data, leading to a need for efficient classification techniques that can manage increasing amounts of information while minimizing storage costs.  The potential increase in data and device variety poses an endless number of possible input features, making variable selection a vital task for maintaining model performance, reducing storage costs, and streamlining processing times for the subsequent training process.  The objective of this study is to investigate, compare, and optimize classification techniques of IoT devices based on a comprehensive set of variables, with a focus on both operational efficiency and economic feasibility.  The authors of this paper conduct an extensive survey of potential variables and then evaluate the effectiveness of different feature selection methods in conjunction with various classification algorithms.  The analysis is performed on two distinct IoT datasets, which are derived from different domains of activity, namely, smart factory and smart home.  The results of this study demonstrate that feature selection prior to classification yields better outcomes compared to methods that combine the two tasks.  Based on the findings of this research, the authors suggest an efficient approach that combines different feature selection techniques to strike a balance between computational efficiency, economic feasibility, and performance efficiency.  The proposed approach is then used to train a classification model that can identify IoT devices with minimal resource consumption, reducing storage costs, and streamlining processing times. Godel modal logics can be interpreted as the non-commutative extension of classical modal logic. This report presents a comparison of different approaches to Godel modal logics with the approaches for KBL and KB4. It also explores Godel modal logics with a connection operator and examines the first-order representations for the basic Godel modal logic and its extensions with a connection operator.

A one-shot learning approach for word alignment is developed, leveraging existing bilingual dictionaries and monolingual texts from the internet. This method proves to be both efficient and effective across 15 language pairs, aligning 90% of words in 10,000-word vocabularies within 2 hours to 2 days. A publicly accessible API provides real-time word alignment for any language pair.

We suggest an iterative algorithm, the Distorted Resolvent Algorithm (DRA), to find Nash equilibria in continuous concave-convex games. By leveraging the properties of the resolvent, DRA ensures a monotonic and contraction-free sequence, converging to a distorted equilibrium that serves as a fixed point of a contractive distortion function. Notably, at optimal settings, the distorted equilibrium coincides with the unique Nash equilibrium, whereas beyond its optimal range, the distorted equilibrium serves as an approximate or "second-best" solution with desirable properties. Furthermore, we establish a criterion for choosing parameters in a way that yields a sequence converging to the true Nash equilibrium in finite time. Our theoretical analysis includes guarantees for both the sequence and its subsequence formed by taking certain averages, showing that these converge to the correct outcome. We also provide an implementation illustration using a specific example of competition.

I will demonstrate the capabilities of the PopSyCLE code, which is a novel tool for computing the properties of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) that comprise Dark Matter (DM). Specifically, I will show how the code can be used to estimate key parameters such as the initial amplitude of perturbations required for PBHs to form the majority of DM, as well as the current-day mass function of PBHs that are trapped in the Milky Way galaxy. The code particularly stands out by incorporating recent theoretical developments that take into account the accretion of nearby subhalos and its effect on PBH mass growth. Furthermore, I will highlight two unique applications of the code: (a) determining the minimum PBH mass that is consistent with observations of binary PBH mergers; and (b) exploring the implications of using PBHs to set a maximum limit on the matter density of the universe.

We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of B molecules with a wedge-shaped structure, formed by combining two B molecules with a D molecule. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we found that in the most wedged systems, phases other than liquid crystalline exhibit a single transition at changing molecule aspect ratios. However, when the molecule structure slightly deviates from a perfect wedge, it results in two transitions at lower molecule aspects but a single transition at higher molecule aspects. In the low molecule aspects range, a hexagonal liquid crystal phase is prevalent, whereas in the high molecule aspects range, a single-liquid phase dominates. We discovered that in the interlying range of molecule aspects, a novel hexagonal liquid crystal phase emerges, characterized by molecule tilt and a 90-degree shift in the director's change rate.

This work investigates spectral representations of stationary Gaussian random fields on the surface of a three-dimensional sphere with no correlation time, utilizing a ladder operator framework. We develop novel explicit formulas for developing random field projections, constructing orthogonal functions, and deriving discrete approximations at any desired level of accuracy. These discrete approximations take the form of a finite sum of squared weighted spherical harmonic coefficients. We demonstrate that the highest order of approximation can be achieved with a finite and arbitrarily small number of terms. Additionally, we provide the explicit order of the number of terms required based on the desired level of accuracy.

A conventional approach to visualizing a quantum state involves measuring the state itself, which typically alters its properties. We have developed a method to overcome this limitation by utilizing interaction-free detection through undetected photons to create a visible representation of a quantum state without disturbing it. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach for both pure and mixed states utilizing a 2D pixelated detector. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the ability to adjust the level of disturbance depending on the desired balance between visualization and state preservation. This technique has the potential to be an essential tool for quantum information processing and research by allowing the visualization of delicate quantum states without introducing errors due to detection.

The interaction between complex liquids and solid surfaces is influenced by various factors including surface roughness and the presence of surfactants. When certain liquids come into contact with a solid, adhesion occurs due to intermolecular forces such as van der Waals forces or surface tension, leading to an increase in contact area between the liquid and the solid. However, if the liquid contains surfactants that lower its surface tension, a specific combination of liquid and solid properties can actually reduce the contact area, a phenomenon that can slow down the liquid's flow and increase friction. We have observed this unique relationship between surface tension and friction in liquid foams using force sensors and a stationary surface with irregularities. The presence of dry soap films led to an increase in friction, whereas adding dilute liquid layers caused friction to decrease before increasing again as the liquid films closed over dry soap film patches. The experiments were conducted with different types of surfaces and temperatures, and the findings are explained through a combination of theoretical aspects related to dry soap films and ELR (van der Waals interactions that occur at shorter ranges).

This research proposes an advanced diagnostic method, combining data enrichment techniques with a deep learning framework, to increase accuracy in skin cancer identification. By integrating the Kayhan Net architecture with BERT, the model surpasses existing benchmarks, achieving a state-of-the-art accuracy of 93.54% on the ISIC dataset by leveraging data augmentation and outlier detection. A novel data augmentation strategy, utilizing spatial transformation, contradicts prevailing best practices, highlighting the complexity of training models on small datasets. Furthermore, the study investigates how different outlier detection methods impact model performance, revealing that entropy-based detection outperforms existing methods.

We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from earlier research. These findings amplify the need for theoretical models more advanced than the random phase approximation. Contrary to the hypothesis suggesting significant acceleration of the carriers due to their interaction with spin fluctuations, our results do not support this theory. Additionally, a comparison with previous electron loss data indicates that sodium's mass enhancement due to dipole-type electron-hole interactions is substantially less than its mass enhancement due to monopole-type interactions measured using ARPES.

Microscopic dynamics is examined in phase space using a novel method that accounts for volume changes and doesn't rely on thermodynamic assumptions. This approach uses the Hamiltonian to transform simulation data into a fixed volume phase space, which can be performed without knowing the Boltzmann constant or temperature. We apply this method to simulations of a system undergoing free expansion, demonstrating that their thermodynamic properties match those of an ideal gas. The proposed method can utilize simulation data generated with any molecular mechanics based potential and doesn't need derivation of an equilibrium distribution function. Therefore, it can be applied to accurately analyze simulation data, particularly in scenarios involving a sudden change in the phase space volume, such as the initial stages of an ideal gas's free expansion.

This article computes the Kontsevich weights of connection and curvature graphs for a symplectic vector field on a finite set of points in the plane, in the specific case where the underlying Poisson structure is given by a 2-form that varies according to a degree-e polynomial. It also establishes a recursive formula for graphs with multiple edges and verifies that this formula aligns with a known universal local Taylor series expansion of the connection and curvature graphs' weights.

This work examines localized modes, referred to as nanoptera, that occur in weakly nonlinear systems consisting of a chain with alternating masses and no external tension. We derive the governing equation for these nanoptera, revealing that their dynamics align with that of a particle moving in a potential landscape defined by the string's nonlinearity. We also investigate the scenario where one mass type has a much larger value, leading to the emergence of robust nanoptera that survive even in highly nonlinear systems.

In principle, primordial features can be detected through their significant effects on the cosmic microwave background anisotropies. This concept, referred to as the Cosmological Collider, yields an observable signal from the collision of nearly light-like particles created during inflationary periods. We are examining the impact of these features on the CMB in search of a more substantial signal, one that could better explain the observed features. To accomplish this, we consider hypothetical scenarios in which massive scalar fields interact with other fields through a mechanism that results in a higher density of states, potentially perceiving features not visible in existing data. Additionally, these scenarios provide a theoretical explanation for the features observed in the Planck data at $\ell = 1430$. We simulate how future experiments such as PRISM and AIRES will be able to detect the signals, and find that with improved sensitivity, we may be able to detect signals with a magnitude of $O(10^{-2})$ microKelvin.

Consider a graph of even order G and its square extension, denoted by square(G). In this analysis, we explore a class of graphs, referred to as accordion graphs, characterized by their property: every edge in square(G) is associated with a unique pair of vertices in G. This class includes the graphs matching certain criteria and all quartic circulant graphs. Our investigation of accordion graphs reveals they possess the following properties: every edge in a graph matching this criterion, denoted by H, is paired; H has a Hamiltonian cycle; H has a pairing of cycles; and two H graphs are identical if and only their corresponding 'tail' graphs are identical. We also determine a general method to identify all quartic circulant graphs matching the criterion. Additionally, we prove that if a graph matching the criterion, denoted by H1, is isomorphic to another graph matching the criterion, denoted by H2, then the corresponding 'tail' graphs of H1 and H2 are also isomorphic. In particular, this means the corresponding 'tail' graphs of H1 and H2 are either exact identical matches or they have no connection at all.

We carry out a detailed analysis of the global behavior of a three-state quantum walk (3SQW) with a $d=3$ and $k=2$ parameter set, where a single marked state is used to define the graph's size, K, and apply a new approach for calculating the 2D quantum walk's scaling behavior. For the first time, we theoretically derive a specific scaling equation that applies to 3SQW and, through numerical simulations, prove that it is also applicable to higher dimensions of 3SQW. Our findings show that this scaling equation accurately predicts the critical conductance and associated correlation length for the 4D, 5D, and 6D cases. Additionally, we find that the behavior of 3SQW lies in an intermediate transition type, displaying a B-B transition type. Although graph symmetry leads to simplified wavefunctions, especially in the Dirac points, this symmetry does not affect the global behavior or transition types.

Our research presents a novel approach to obtaining feature representations from Vision Transformer (ViT) using self-supervised learning methods. In contrast to existing self-supervised ViT methods, we introduce the EmerginG AttributEs (GEA) framework which generates emergent features from raw image data through a distillation process that preserves low-level visual characteristics and high-level semantic information. The key features of our GEA framework are symmetric data augmentations, a multi-level distillation pipeline, and the use of an embedding vector to guide loss assignment in the self-supervised process. The outcome is a robust image representation that can be utilized for both image-level classification and semantic segmentation tasks, and which exhibits superior performance compared to other self-supervised ViT methods and traditional convolutional neural networks. The source code for our GEA framework is available at https://github.com/simbo88/GEA.

A new cosmological model, known as the Dissipative Unified Dark Substance (DUDS), is presented to address the current observed phenomena of the universe, such as acceleration, dark matter, dark energy, and gravitational waves. This model postulates two interdependent DUDS components, A and B, interacting through the exchange of temporal and spatial momentum, thereby constraining the universe's evolution. By determining key cosmological parameters, we find the DUDS model fits within the Planck 2018 cosmological framework, providing a statistically significant improvement. Furthermore, we show that the phase transition from the dark energy phase of component A to the dark matter phase, accompanied by a non-zero coefficient governing the universe's expansion, is compatible with the observed cosmic acceleration. In addition, we identify a specific momentum value at the moment of matter-radiation equilibrium, and the model's phase transition from dark energy to dark matter occurs approximately 3.4 billion years after the matter-radiation equilibrium.

We offer a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of H\"older spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

The community-driven creator platform has made it possible for content to be generated in various forms, such as images and videos, using text prompts, which can then be manipulated by users to produce unique variations. However, this led to a major issue of abuse, particularly by those generating harmful content, which prompted the need for a more stable and meaningful representation of content in latent space. Our research at Adobe Research aims to address this challenge, having identified key requirements for developing this semantic space. We propose the Stable Creator, an innovative system that meets these needs, allowing any user to produce consistent variations of content by providing minimal input, which we demonstrate through its effective implementation in both image and video generation models.

This research introduces an innovative technique known as reversible concealment that enables a hidden observer to a visual data stream to deduce an underlying target, while ensuring that the associated observations remain confidential. We develop an efficient solution that relies on Bayesian Neural Networks functioning in an adversarial capacity, where the utility of additional data for target inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we create low-energy theories based on effective field theories for general neutrino interactions and a specific type of dark matter called a vector fermion. We utilize experimental limits set by J=ψ visible and invisible decay rates as well as observations of neutrino less decays to construct and analyze these theories. We then compare our findings to current constraints on neutrino less decays derived from J/ψ data and future sensitivity projections from J=ψ experiments, as well as other studies. We also investigate the consequences of detecting a signal in J/ψ searches for dark matter, given existing and anticipated limits from J=ψ experiments. We our analysis for sterile neutrinos reveals that J/ψ invisible decay constraints enhance existing conclusions from cosmology and J=ψ visible decay data, ruling out large portions of parameter space. We also find that future sensitivity projections do not significantly alter the conclusion. Assuming the standard model completeness for J=ψ invisible decay, we find that J/ψ data strongly limits the mass and interaction scale of the vector fermion dark matter model, given current and anticipated limits, as its key parameter approaches a singularity.

The sun's outer atmosphere, known as the corona, has a temperature that surpasses millions of degrees, which has puzzled scientists for a long time. One factor that could be driving these high temperatures is the presence of complex and concentrated magnetic fields within the sun's active regions. The study of a specific active region on the sun's surface provided evidence for the existence of small, bright areas with high field strengths. These areas, which are much smaller than the surrounding resolution, displayed a distinct pattern in the flow of light and heat. The data revealed a significant gap in the distribution of brightness within these areas, which cannot be explained by the usual light and heat patterns in the sun. The observed gap was accompanied by a substantial increase in the sun spots' surface area. The proposed theory to describe this phenomenon is based on the idea that the sun spots are comprised of intricate and complex magnetic field structures. The evidence suggests that these areas are likely to be part of larger and more complex magnetic field structures that are temporarily fixed in place.

Human vision is known to rapidly process motion, yet it's unclear how this is achieved, particularly when recognizing complex objects. Research has shown that both biological and artificial models can exploit constraints to efficiently interpret motion, though the most effective approach for dynamic object recognition remains unclear. Specifically, it's unknown whether 2D or 3D representations provide the greatest computational benefits. To address this question, we examined minimal films captured by a portable, low-power camera, effectively creating a simplified dataset of 3D object movements. Our analysis compared the difficulty of distinguishing between two objects in 2D versus 3D contexts and found that dynamic recognition was generally easier in 3D settings. Additionally, we found that both simple and complex 3D scenes posed similar interpretation challenges, suggesting that the increased complexity of these scenes does not significantly affect dynamic object recognition. Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that 3D representation supports more efficient dynamic object recognition, suggesting that this format could offer an advantage for real-time object detection applications.

Long-standing, weak, and widespread cosmic strings theory generated by symmetry breaking at high energy levels, predicted the existence of topological magnetic monopoles, which are supported by both quantum theory and string theory. However, large-scale cosmic structures, such as galaxy clusters and the cosmic web, do not have the magnetic monopoles detected as expected, based on breaking of scale invariance. We propose that milli-magnetically charged dark matter, which is of the form of isolated monopoles or fragmented fragments, can explain this phenomenon. As dark matter, it is able to evade detection by standard methods but can effectively interact with normal matter through weak and electromagnetic forces, particularly during temporary periods of ionization. This interaction occurs when dark matter, which has a very low velocity, passes through gas clouds in the developing galaxy, causing it to polarize and maintain a residual magnetic field that persists to the present. We provide a mathematical equation that describes how this process works and offer a connection to observations of distant galaxy rotation, which relies on data collected by the Tully-Fisher. We also provide a mathematical range for the predicted magnetic monopole density, which is determined by the condition of neither excessive galaxy rotation speed nor excessive cosmic microwave background radiation. We also provide a mathematical range for the predicted magnetic monopole density, which is determined by the condition of neither excessive galaxy rotation speed nor excessive cosmic microwave background radiation.

The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research area has immense potential to utilize AI in real-time weather forecasting. This work addresses the challenge of accurate weather prediction by leveraging the video transformer framework. Building on the success of the transformer model, we integrated SWCA into VT, allowing for the generation of a precise weather prediction output. By utilizing vision transformer with a novel shift window cross-attention module, we produced a high-quality output, achieving a significant increase of approximately 7% over the baseline model.

In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a basis can be found where the symmetry prevents coupling, leading to viable dark matter candidates. Specifically, we analyze the $S_3$-symmetric three-Higgs-doublet models that allow softly broken $S_3$ terms, determining which models can host dark matter. After eliminating scenarios resulting in unstable VEVs, we're left with two candidates: one involving a neutral Higgs and two charged Higgses, and another with three neutral Higgses. We discover that in the first case, dark matter is consistently represented by a mixture of neutral Higgses, whereas in the second case, it's often represented by a light complex state arising from a mixture of Higgses and a family-dependent dark matter candidate. Assuming a simplified unitary unit, we're able to bound parameter spaces that host dark matter, finding that in the first case, dark matter is better represented by a neutral Higgs for heavier masses greater than around 30 GeV.

The quadrilateral conjecture was revised as the PPT quadrilateral conjecture, and we discuss its current status. The PPT conjecture's evidence indicates it's likely true, but the PPT quadrilateral conjecture remains largely unsolved.

In this research, we address the need for an efficient computational method that captures how a neuron regulates the transport of substances along its axis, a process important for delivering nutrients and waste products. We frame this challenge as an optimization problem subject to partial differential equations that model the movement of substances. These equations are adapted to account for the nervous system's unique geometry, with a focus on the axon's structure. We introduce a novel approach that uses a sparse collection of points to approximate the profile of substances being transported and develop a variational formulation based on this approximation, leading to a sparse matrix representation of the governing equations. This matrix is then reduced to a smaller size through the use of a Kontorovich-GMC penalty term. Our method enables the efficient handling of a large number of sources and sinks within the boundary of the axon, as well as adjustments to their locations to match observed profiles. This is demonstrated through numerical simulations of different neuron geometries, using adaptive mesh refinement to ensure accurate results.

The effective management of limited resources in complex systems, such as businesses and economies, heavily relies on time-sensitive decisions made at the intersection of finance, politics, and social interactions. Typically, these systems can be represented as network diagrams, where specific patterns, known as strong and weak Loopy Random Networks, emerge in their node interconnections. However, it is the unique presence of these connections, rather than the underlying topology, that sets them apart. In our research, we establish a method to capture and characterize the transient patterns in these systems, referring to their temporal variations as the system's temporal margin. This work is particularly relevant to the world of finance, where trading patterns vary significantly over time.

In a binary system consisting of a white dwarf and a black hole, we investigate the interaction between a falling white dwarf and its surrounding accretion disk. We find that the white dwarf's surface material will be attracted by the black hole, leading to a significant emission of gravitational waves as it nears the point of no return. Approximately 0.001 seconds before the white dwarf reaches this point, the entire mass will be condensed into a disk at 99% of the Einstein radius. The subsequent emission from the accretion disk will take on the character of a standard multi-temperature blackbody spectrum, with the Eddington limit providing an upper bound on the emitted energy. We calculate that the peak energy of the emitted photons will be in the range of 10-100 keV, and the total energy released will be in the order of 10^41-10^48 ergs, depending on the distance between the white dwarf and the black hole. The material dropped by the white dwarf will first experience intense hydraulic fracturing, followed by a prolonged period of diffusive spreading, during which time most of its energy will be released in the form of electromagnetic and gravitational waves.

Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions between a lepton, quarks, and mesons or baryons, can provide insight into the hadronic structure of these hadrons. To investigate the internal compositions of these hadrons, we use form factors to express the hadronic parts of the amplitudes governing the $\tau$-decays into final states containing one particle and a lepton. To calculate these form factors, which describe the hadronic currents, we apply sum rules in local quantum field theory. Our recent studies focused on the $a_1(1260)$ and $h_1(1895)$ mesons, but for the purpose of completeness, we will outline the general framework for calculating form factors in three-body $\tau$-decays involving baryons here.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with $k$ and $\ell$ being positive integers where the exponential functions' bases are greater than 2, and investigated their behavior as either $k$ or $\ell$ approaches infinity while their sum remains constant. This research further explores those measures for specific values of $k$ and $\ell$, including scenarios where they equal 1, which recovers the Jaccard distance. Conversely, setting $k$ equal to $\ell$ yields an original metric; applying the method of normalized information distance from Kolmogorov (1986) reveals that this new metric reduces to a form equivalent to the Wang and Weng additive information distance.

Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on the quality of their synthetic data, as high-quality pairs are hard to obtain in real-world scenarios, while an excessive amount of pairs is difficult for the model to effectively utilize. We observed that existing approaches neglect the variations within a single blurry image, treating each pixel independently without considering the interdependence of motion across the scene, which hinders the motion deblurring model's performance. To address this issue, we developed a novel training framework that utilizes a pseudo-blur synthesizer module to generate plausible clear images from blurry inputs. The proposed approach leverages the video sequence's inherent properties, incorporating both the scene-dependent and object-specific motion variations, which enables it to outperform existing methods significantly.
