In synthetic biology, designing pre-defined functional molecular circuits is the primary objective, with applications in bioengineering where tissue-like systems can make informative decisions. A notable example on the table is the development of a toggle switch, a basic cellular logic circuit that has been successfully implemented in various organisms. Building upon this foundation, researchers now aim to create more complex molecular systems, such as tunable spiking neural networks, to simulate neural behavior and potentially lead to innovative biohybrid robotic technologies. A neural circuit, for instance, could be designed to learn and memorize, like a classical, digital computer, or even outperform it by leveraging biological characteristics, such as decentralized processing or adaptive learning. Here, the possibilities of developing advanced molecular systems, using neuroinspired architectures, are explored, along with the challenges and potential applications, such as the creation of a universal, Turing-complete molecular computational system, possibly with superior performance capabilities to conventional electronic computers.

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to have any two elements within it that are close together in the original set to be equivalent in the new set, effectively acting as a measure of how 'dense' the set is. When this openness does not exist, the set is completely dense in its own ultrapower, meaning that a perfect copy of the set itself can always be found within it. It has been shown that the various forms of openness in a set all work together to provide a complete classification system for how dense the set is in its own ultrapower. This classification system also reveals a deeper relationship between the set itself and its ultrapower that had not been previously recognized.

The growing cost of training Deep Learning models is a pressing concern for organizations. To optimize this process, researchers have long relied on general purpose benchmarking, which compares model architectures on a specific dataset. Yet, recent advancements in hardware and software have created opportunities for more personalized approaches. In our research, we demonstrate the effectiveness of dataset-specific profiling, a method that focuses on evaluating the unique characteristics of a dataset to inform model optimization. Our findings, guided by theoretical modeling and supported by experimental results, show that benchmarking alone is insufficient for optimizing training Deep Learning models. Additionally, the most efficient methods of dataset profiling depend closely on the dataset's features. Our empirical analysis verifies the feasibility and precision of our proposed profiling methods, yielding significant improvements in inference latency, throughput, and energy consumption, in cases where batch sizes vary greatly.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph of order t. This has been verified for complete graphs, four-color inputs, and those with five colors, except for the five-color circuit family. In this research, we demonstrate that all non-bipartite five-color circuits have a complete graph of order five within them, and all five-color tournaments have a complete graph of order five. We further prove that if a graph can be colored with five colors and has no complete graph of order five, then it contains a complete graph of order four that is two-colored.

This research introduces an advanced algorithm for restoring smooth graph signals, utilizing a generalized form of the correntropy metric that incorporates the effects of noise. A specific kernel function, capable of effectively capturing the properties of laplacian kernels, enables the derivation of a closed-form solution for the estimation of the original signal values at unseen nodes. However, this approach suffers from a significant drawback - the need for pre-specified kernel parameters - and relies on an oversimplified assumption about the properties of the underlying graph. In an effort to overcome this limitation, we propose modifying the kernel parameters of an existing graph signal reconstruction algorithm, utilizing an adaptive learning approach for the parameters of a kernel function that is compatible with the generalized correntropy. This new algorithm is capable of being implemented in real-time, as it relies on a single iterative update equation. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms the existing method and a competing approach known as the generalized mean-absolute deviation method. Furthermore, we investigate the theoretical conditions under which the proposed algorithm can converge to a accurate estimate of the original graph signal.

Theoretical and experimental research on entangled spinor Bose-Einstein condensates has been conducted to design a method to produce specific quantum states despite widespread background noise in detection equipment. By investigating two common types of background noise, it was found that deep inner-shell excitations of the spinor components could provide a solution. Both the impact of background noise caused by excitation of spin and orbital motions and the methods to overcome them have been studied in detail. Additionally, the applicability of these findings to other systems has been considered.

The purpose of this research paper is to derive sharp, quantitative estimates for the first eigenvalue of the first Robin eigenvalue problem involving the $p$-Laplace operator. This problem seeks to find the maximum and minimum values of the first eigenvalue $\lambda_p(\Omega, \beta)$ given a bounded domain $\Omega$ in n-dimensional space and a bounded function $\beta$. Previously, quantitative estimates for this problem under specific conditions on $\beta$ had been established. The current research builds upon existing estimates by providing sharp bounds for the first eigenvalue when the second eigenvalue is known. Additionally, the results account for various boundary conditions, including Neumann and Dirichlet scenarios.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have attained remarkable success in processing complex, non-linear data, particularly in signal processing applications. However, the graph convolutional neural network (GCNN) has distinct characteristics compared to traditional convolutional neural networks used for image processing. The unique graph convolution operation confers to GCNN its ability to efficiently handle graph-structured data. Yet, the implicit and abstract nature of the graph convolution operation hinders a thorough comprehension of its functioning, making it challenging to expand GCNN to other domains. Consequently, we propose an intuitive interpretation of the graph convolution operation by adapting the classical matched filter concept, offering a deeper understanding of GCNN. Our study reveals that the graph convolution operation can be viewed as a weighted, conditional averaging process. The developed analysis provides a solid foundation for the development of novel graph convolutional block architectures and generalization to other structured data such as grids and trees. The proposed approach is validated by comparing its performance with existing state-of-the-art methods on various graph-related machine learning tasks.

Despite the success achieved by recurrent neural network-based models in dependency parsing, they are unable to capture long-term dependencies efficiently. In response, various models that utilize self-attention, including neural dependency parsers with multi-task learning capabilities, have been developed to extract contextualized dependencies from input sentences. In applications requiring small datasets, these models struggle to capture contextualized dependencies due to the limitations of their training data. In an effort to overcome this limitation, a novel approach, Deep Contextualized Self-learning (DCS), is introduced to improve contextualized dependency parsing in data-scarce scenarios by leveraging contextualized representations. This method iteratively trains two sequential models - a neural neural dependency parser and a self-attention-based parser - on each other's outputs, iteratively refining contextualized dependencies. Experiments on 23 languages from various datasets demonstrate that DCS achieves significant enhancements over conventional neural dependency parsers, with improvements rising up to 111%. Additionally, DCS shows robustness across a wide range of NLP applications.

We use the self-consistent light front quark model to calculate the transition form factors for the process $B \to D\ell\nu_\ell$ at different quark momentum fractions. Our results show good agreement with Bayesian analysis and other approaches, but differ from Drell-Yan frame instanton model and soft collision model predictions. The outcome also sheds light on the role of the $B \to D$ current matrix elements in this process.

We use the example of the bosonic string theory's tachyon action to illustrate how certain unconventional gauge symmetries, which violate conventional braiding rules, can lead to counterintuitive outcomes in the context of brane dynamics. Specifically, our analysis reveals that the presence of these unconventional symmetries causes the tachyon action to be multiply connected, leading to conflicts with string theory's global consistency when considered at specific points within the moduli space. Additionally, we explore the implications of these symmetries on the existing solutions within the tachyon action and propose connections to other areas of research, such as quantum mechanics and black hole physics.

We demonstrate in this research paper a direct link between choiceless polynomial time, symmetric circuits, and a particular class of digraphs as previously described by Barrington, Marion, and Tassarongna. Furthermore, we establish at least two distinct circuits that are both non-monotone and of degree two, yet exhibit different structures - one is invariant in direction, the other is not, resolving a query posed by Kaufmann and Sch{\"o}nigh{\"o}fer. In our analysis, we also present an alternative proof for a previously established upper limit by Tassarongna, this time using a concept from the study of digraphs. Additionally, we address two not previously explored issues - first, we derive an upper limit for the amount of time required to solve the Halting Problem using symmetric circuits of a specified size when the underlying digraph is in a particular class; second, we investigate how non-deterministic circuits of a certain size can be constructed from a linearly structured non-deterministic Turing machine that is context-free and runs in a specified amount of time.

In the pyrochlore iridates, series compounds Eu_1-xBi_xIr2O7, exhibit unique quantum properties originating from the interplay of unusual geometric and magnetic correlations. Bi-doped Eu2Ir2O7 shows an insulating-to-metal transition as the Bi content increases. To investigate this transition further, we employed hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy and observed a significant increase in charge localization with Bi doping. Interestingly, at x = 0.5, we saw a sudden drop in charge localization and the concomitant emergence of a self-energy peak at approximately 2 eV, coinciding with the onset of metallic behavior. Additionally, at higher Bi concentrations (x = 0.6 and 0.7), we detected a self-energy peak at lower binding energies, positioned near a known feature at 0.5 eV, attributed to Ir 5d hybridization. These findings suggest that charge localization in Eu_1-xBi_xIr2O7 is stabilized up to x = 0.5, amounting to approximately 10% doping.

Consider a metric space ${\mathfrak M}=({\mathcal M},\rho)$ and a Banach space $X$, with a set-valued mapping $F$ that maps ${\mathcal M}$ to the family ${\mathcal K}_m(X)$ of compact convex subsets of $X$ of dimension $m$ or less. Our recent joint research with Charles Fefferman established a principle that allows for Lipschitz selection of mappings like $F$, provided they satisfy specific growth constraints. This paper presents a metric interpretation of the principle, leading to a simplified standard for Lipschitz selections in lower dimensional settings. It also explores applications of the principle to derive convergence results for iterations of set-valued mappings and solves associated problems in categories ${\mathcal C}^{0}$ and ${\mathcal C}^{1}$.

The objectives of this research are two-fold. Firstly, we explore the possibilities of constructing likelihoods that exhibit cyclic and non-transitive properties. Preliminary findings suggest that likelihoods tend to be transitive, however, we hypothesize that this may not always be the case, and a deeper investigation is required. Secondly, we examine the implications of encountering likelihood ratios with cyclic properties in the context of hypothesis testing, and find that such instances do not necessarily preclude model discrimination. Moreover, we suggest that the non-transitive nature of likelihood ratios could be advantageous in choosing between statistical models.

A compelling case can be made that runtime code generation enhances the reach of modern software development, yet it introduces complexities that can impede code transparency and reproducibility. Although compile-time techniques offer a viable solution to address these issues, they are generally confined to a limited set of applications. We contend that a specific compile-time approach, namely run-time code generation guided by specifications, can be applied across a broader spectrum of runtime code generation methodologies. By systematically evaluating the extent of compatibility, we identified four challenges that can impede the application of compile-time techniques to runtime code generation. Our concurrent implementation of an open-source tool successfully addressed these limitations, thereby demonstrating the practical feasibility of incorporating a compile-time specializer to optimize runtime code generation efficiently.

Light-weight, geometrically complex, and high-technology Direct-Detection experiments may be able to directly observe sub-GeV dark matter interacting with normal matter via the nuclear scattering process. In particular, large numbers of electron recoil signals at the MeV energy scale could serve as an indication of dark matter present in such experiments. This would require significant improvement to the current experimental limits, specifically in the low-energy range, in order to confirm whether dark matter is indeed interacting with normal matter in this manner.

This paper presents a theoretical analysis of a anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, characterized by the interaction of a two-level system and a quantized electromagnetic field, in the presence of coupling between $s$ and $|00\rangle$ states. Following initial conditions where both the atom and field are in a superposition of $\pm 1$ and $\pm n$ states, respectively, we examine Rabi oscillations, entanglement, and transmission in two specific scenarios: with and without initial entanglement of the atom and field. Our analysis focuses on two situations: (i) strong coupling and (ii) weak coupling between the atom and field. Our findings show that when the atom and field are not initially entangled, a specific value of $n$ can lead to complete transmission, while if they are initially entangled, no such condition applies and transmission decreases with increasing entanglement. We also found that for strong coupling, no transmission occurs and the Rabi oscillations disappear. Conversely, for weak coupling, a distinct Rabi oscillation pattern persists even when the atom and field are initially entangled.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from complex signals is challenging due to interference from motion noise, particularly in patients with a high risk of heart disease who are also undergoing physical activity. Our research presents an innovative approach to IBI estimation that leverages a Tiramisu convolutional neural network model. Unlike traditional methods which rely on signal frequency domain analysis and time domain features including R-peak, our novel strategy directly estimates IBIs from R-peak locations without requiring time-domain feature extraction, facilitating real-time implementation on devices. We tested our model on the public INTERHHB database, showcasing its superior performance over existing methods with an average absolute error of 11.55ms, and highlighting its potential to provide immediate alerts for patients at risk of heart disease.

We examine the theoretical framework and statistical properties of a active Brownian particle undergoing changes in position, force, and friction over time in a one and two-dimensional space. The phase graph of these variations exhibits patterns that are distinct from those of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, even in the presence of constant movement forces. Our analysis reveals the existence of three separate stationary states, each corresponding to a specific work rate regime. The statistical properties of the work increments were found to be non-stationary and not correlated in space, leading to an absence of long-term dependence. The research may serve as a theoretical foundation for modeling active biological particles and confirming recent experimental findings.

The integration of gesture recognition capabilities into robots and computer systems has the potential to significantly enhance their ability to interact with humans in a variety of settings, including entertainment, education, and as assistive tools. To reach this point, a comprehensive and detailed dataset of multiview gesture data is needed to support the development of advanced deep learning algorithms. This paper presents HUMBI, a large-scale dataset consisting of 57,750 video sequences captured from three different viewpoints and featuring complex, diverse human body movements. To utilize this data, a set of advanced multiview gesture recognition models is introduced, which achieve impressive results on hidden testing datasets. This research ultimately leads to the establishment of a competitive challenge to further advance the field. The HUMBI dataset is accessible at https://xjliu95.github.io/HUMBI/.

Although numerous studies have tested the cross-lingual transfer in NLP, there is still a significant gap in understanding the implementation details of this transfer. We conducted an extensive study involving 11 languages and achieved notable gains across 7 NLP tasks by utilizing the annotations of a single high-resource language (English). We achieved this improvement by mapping task definitions from English to other languages, leveraging either monolingual or bilingual word embeddings. Our results showed that the representation of task definitions in English is weakly connected to the performances of other languages, indicating that it can serve as a guiding abstraction for model-agnostic cross-lingual transfer. We made our code and data sets publically available.

A landmark video super-resolution technique known as BasicVSR has set a new standard for the field, yielding the best results in the VSR challenge at the ICCV 2021, surpassing other top-in-class models. This success is attributed to BasicVSR's efficient 4-division parallel architecture, achieving exceptional video super-resolution results with high quality and efficiency. However, the original approach has several shortcomings that hinder its performance, such as an overly simplistic propagation method, inadequate feature alignment, and a suboptimal decoder design. We developed a series of improvements to these aspects, incorporating them into a new model, BasicVSR++, which demonstrates a substantial improvement over the original model. BasicVSR++ outperforms BasicVSR by a significant margin, and even surpasses several top-performing models in the VSR challenge. The source code for BasicVSR++ is publicly available at https://github.com/Dr0pS0n4ry/BasicVSR.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using a shared policy can lead to catastrophic interference, where the performance of one task severely hampers the others. We've found that using model-based approaches, which learn environment dynamics models and policy models, can address this issue. However, implementing such methods is challenging due to the absence of theoretical guarantees for learning both policy and dynamics in multi-task settings. We've developed a modular network architecture that learns policies, dynamics, and value functions in a multi-task RL context, and proves that it provides a stable solution with optimal performance. We also show that this approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multiple challenging environments.

Two key factors drive the widespread use of heat engines: their high efficiency and the ability to operate over long periods of time. In search of better performance, researchers have been developing new heat engines with specific properties, such as guaranteed output levels or fixed operating speeds, by limiting the ways in which the engine can be controlled. Despite these restrictions, it has been found that it is always possible to optimize the engine's performance by maximizing the work per heat with minimal thermal energy wasted in the process. We found that the optimal control technique relies on the minimum time required to reach the target state, rather than the rate at which heat is exchanged with the surroundings. Furthermore, the protocol often becomes a 'power-on' situation where the engine runs at maximum speed as soon as it starts. In many cases, the optimal operation of the engine consumes the maximum amount of heat possible from the hot reservoir, leading to a protocol with a straightforward 'heat-in' and 'expel-excess-heat' pattern that is quick and efficient.

This research proposes a preliminary investigation into the effects of hurricanes and storm surges on power systems through spatial analysis. To achieve this, we integrated a spatial model of hurricane-induced damage to infrastructure, derived from historical data and genetic algorithms, into a model of combined electric power transfer and flow. Our case study focused on the Northeast US power system and used real data from the National Hurricane Center to simulate potential scenarios for which we optimized solutions to minimize total power loss across the system. It's crucial to note that these models were developed in a research environment and are intended to facilitate further investigation rather than provide practical solutions for real-world applications.

This research proves a hypothesis known as the three balls conjecture for functions of n-dimensional space Clifford analyzed under harmonic analysis principles. The investigation focuses particularly on functions of n-dimensional space subject to specific transformation rules, known as Clifford algebra monogenic functions, in relation to their behavior within three interconnected spaces. Proving this hypothesis involves verifying that these functions adhere to a specific inequality when their values are compared at the center of three interconnected balls to their values at three distinct points separated by a common radius. Additionally, the study establishes the essential inequality, a crucial step towards verifying the three balls conjecture, which will likely have significant implications in understanding the behavior of functions in n-dimensional space for n equal to or greater than two.

We undertook a detailed study of the Heterochaos baker map's phase space dynamics, particularly focusing on a specific invariant set derived from the Dyck system. This set consists of sequences satisfying a specific grammatical rule and, when mapped, reveals two distinct modes of entropy increase. Initially, it appears that the system's entropy grows in a predictable manner, following a plot that can be accurately modeled. However, once the system crosses a critical threshold, its entropy begins to increase at a much faster rate, with the map's sensitivity (or Lyapunov exponent) providing a useful point of comparison. We found that the rapid shift in entropy growth is not solely the result of the system's parameters, but rather is influenced by a combination of factors, including the sequences' lengths and a critical threshold in the system's complexity. Notably, this phenomenon is not unique to the Heterochaos baker map, with similar behavior observed in other systems, such as the 1-dimensional logistic map. The discovery of this feature highlights the system's tendency to make a "decision" between two different modes of behavior, with implications for our understanding of the system's dynamics in both the low and high entropy regimes.

The potential of the expanded scalar sectors of beyond Standard Model theories will be examined across three potential scenarios using simulation methods. These simulations will be performed using Monte Carlo event generators at two different future collider configurations, the 33 TeV high-luminosity large hadron collider and a 25 TeV future hadron collider. The theories examined include a single scalar extension of the Standard Model and two scenarios of weakly coupled scalar-compositeness models, with the latter featuring a $SU(5)$-based gauge extension. The analysis will focus on the full simulation outcomes to determine the most efficient detection approaches for the desired signals, which will then be compared to the predictions from leading-order theories. The results indicate that even with the most advanced detection techniques, the expanded collider configurations will still face significant challenges in differentiating the theories from the Standard Model at the early stages of the experiment. However, at higher luminosity thresholds, the signal patterns will resemble those predicted by the amplitudes of the underlying theories, which will be within reach with the high luminosity conditions. The future hadron collider is likely to be able to detect the signals from the Standard Model and weakly coupled scalar-compositeness theory even with lower luminosity conditions. Additionally, the analysis reveals that the current event generators are still insufficiently developed for the expanded collider programs, particularly in the post-production stage, and urge theorists and experimenters to work together to create more realistic simulated events that accurately represent the theoretical predictions.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent filter banks. WN suffers from increased complexity and computational challenges as it tries to model the nuances of speech/music data directly. Our solution involves modifying the convolutional layer in WN to incorporate pitch-dependent filter banks, along with introducing semi-autoregressive structure to the model for more efficient training. Our experiments indicate that QPNet outperforms WN in terms of convergence speed, model size and distortion, with the added benefit of being able to control spectral period. Our code is available online at the specified URL.

To handle the inherent complexities of preference data, including preference locality, sparse ratings, and subjective opinions, this research proposes a novel bicluster-based recommendation framework. The collaborative filtering method we develop leverages both item-based and user-based aspects, incorporating preference patterns in a pairwise manner across dimensions. Our approach can be viewed as an extension of existing bicluster-based methods, achieving better performance by considering all possible pairwise relationships, utilizing sparse data, and addressing preference diversity. Our method's efficacy is demonstrated by our experiments, which show superior recommendation performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, including exclusive, incremental, and deep learning-based recommendations, on three real-world datasets.

The sun's high-level magnetic activity significantly affects its characteristic features, making the sun's behavior unique among other stars. By utilizing the HARPS-N solar telescope, astronomers have collected extensive data on the sun's activity, allowing for extensive analysis of its properties. By using these data, researchers have discovered that certain features of the sun's activity are comparable to those of other stars, while others are distinct. Interestingly, the sun's activity features show variations at frequencies below 1 Hz, which aren't seen in sunspot-related data. This has sparked the idea that these low-frequency fluctuations might be attributed to the sun's facular brightnings. By incorporating the sun's new behavior into established activity features, researchers have developed indicators such as the Displacement Index and the Time Distance, which effectively utilize all available information. This includes low-frequency data, making them more efficient than previous methods. While the new indices show minimal improvements for active stars with moderate levels of activity, they offer significant enhancements for both highly active and less active stars.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, we suggest a new approach. Since Majorana-induced peaks at zero energy can be split by resistance variations, we propose using a setup involving a resistive electrode coupled to a host material with a gap. The distinct peak splitting patterns resulting from Ohmic dissipation in this type of setup should differ significantly for Majorana and competing theories. Moreover, the intensity ratios of Majorana-induced and competing peaks should respond differently to temperature and they should exhibit distinct responses to non-Ohmic losses. Following a theoretical framework, we demonstrate the feasibility of distinguishing Majorana signs through a simple experiment involving a resistive tunneling measurement at non-zero temperatures.

Mark Kisin introduced the concept of B-K-marked algebraic stacks as a B-K-marked space's analog, ultimately establishing that B-K-marked spaces are equivalent to B-K-marked algebraic stacks. Building upon this, B-K-marked spaces can now be replaced by B-K-marked spaces with locally unramified marks in various applications, specifically in the study of local-global principles and stable homotopy theory. In the case of Picard delooping theory, B-K-marked spaces can be further generalized to Picard-B Marked spaces by employing the B-Picard algebraic space Pic_d. By doing so, this paper proves that B-K-marked spaces are essentially equivalent to B-K-marked spaces with locally unramified marks, and also shows that B-K-marked spaces can be reinterpreted as B-K Marked spaces for any B. Additionally, the author explores an extension of the concept B-K Marked space, specifically in situations where B is a subalgebra of A, and then applies these new definitions to theories based on the B-K Marked space.

A current trend in image editing techniques utilizes reference images and style guides, enabling the creation of edited images and their associated styles, but the process often omits the aspect of reproducing image colors. A novel approach, known as Global Forward and Inverse Hue Mapping (GF IH), was developed to address this color reproduction shortfall in image editing techniques. GF IH incorporates a hue-based mapping mechanism that accounts for both the angle and radius of hue segments, making it more precise and effective compared to existing methods. GF IH's efficiency is further highlighted by its ability to be computed in a single pass, unlike existing methods. GF IH's effectiveness is demonstrated through qualitative evaluations on various natural image datasets, showcasing its capabilities to reproduce image colors with higher accuracy. A comparison of GF IH's performance with existing methods reveals its superior performance, with its code and data repositories providing the necessary support for the research community.

This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC contest at the 35th International Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, 2022, held during the 1st Joint Workshop on Video Question Answering and Auxiliary Tasks for Vision. The contest focused on generating the text description of the question being asked in a video, which falls under the category of video question answering (VQA). Our research involves developing a modular approach to tackle this problem, employing the BERT language model and making use of the most visually significant frames from the given video to obtain the relevant context. Moreover, this technical report provides detailed insights into the dataset analysis and the results obtained from the robust ensemble of the proposed models, which yielded the top performance in the contest with a Char FREME score of 81.34, outperforming the runner-up by 1.04 and greatly surpassing the baseline by 81.34 and 34.86 in terms of BLEU-4 score. Notably, this model achieved the highest human parity in the dataset with a score of 51.15 and showed strong geometric location accuracy with a score of 81.34.

In snowstorms, heavy snowfall is influenced by strong winds, greatly affecting the snow's fall speed and pattern. Research has found that atmospheric turbulence has a significant impact on snowfall, but the exact details of its influence on snowfall are still not fully understood. Our study uses high-resolution videos captured at the base of a snowfall event to investigate the selective sweeping hypothesis, which suggests that larger snowflakes move faster than smaller ones, causing them to be blown by the wind in a direction perpendicular to their initial trajectory. Our research reveals that at a certain height, the smaller snowflakes are indeed being blown backwards while the larger ones continue falling straight down, confirming the selective sweeping hypothesis. Our findings can help improve the modeling of snowfall, ultimately aiding in weather forecasting.

As robots carry out tasks such as delivering goods and taking photos, there are growing concerns about their potential role in spreading diseases like COVID-19. In response to these concerns, many governments have imposed restrictions on people moving around. These travel limitations affect robots as well, particularly those designed for exploration and navigation. In an effort to comply with current guidelines, we suggest a novel approach known as deep active prediction, where a robot utilizes forecasting instead of its usual navigation capabilities. By predicting the future state of the environment, the robot can determine if it will be permitted to move to a particular location. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our deep active prediction approach through tests in both simulated and real-world environments, utilizing a SUAS robot.

In the field of particle physics, researchers need to process vast amounts of data produced by detectors at various experiments. This paper focuses on the Sparse Time Projection chamber's data reduction challenges and introduces an innovative solution – the Bicephalous Convolutional Autoencoder. This autoencoder, comprising a convolutional autoencoder for projection images and a recurrent autoencoder for time-ordered data, effectively reduces data while retaining key features about the physics events. Its bicephalous structure allows it to efficiently operate at high speeds, making it suitable for use cases requiring rapid data reduction at a level of 98% or more. Its performance, with a 97.68% reduction in data size, outperforms alternative methods while maintaining 98% or more of the essential event features.

Utilizing the Finzi gravity model, we've obtained a self-consistent equation for the radial density distribution of galaxy clusters. We then compared our results with the Navarro-Frenk-White model by calculating the resulting beta profiles and conventional analysis parameters such as concentration-mass relations, and seed mass estimates based on the concentration-mass relations. We discovered that the beta parameters derived from the Finzi model are comparable to those of the NFW model, yet the predicted concentration-mass relations and seed mass estimates are distinct. We claim that the discrepancies between the two predictions arise primarily from the differing radial density profiles of the two models, specifically the differing radial accretion rates. We verified that the beta parameters are closely tied to the radial accretion rates, which in turn are determined by the specific gravity model in use. We suggest that the NFW-based theoretical predictions of concentration-mass relations and seed mass estimates may not adequately describe the observed trends in galaxy clusters, and that the Finzi model is a potential alternative.

A type of geometric hypergraph called d-dimensional convex geometric hypergraph, PGHd(n), consists of a collection of d-dimensional convex subsets, where each subset contains at least one element. This study explores a problem related to the saturation number of PGHd(n) using a combinatorial approach and provides an upper bound which is nearly optimal in dimension one, with the goal of understanding the general case.

To understand how p-p correlations develop within the region of alpha particle formation, researchers investigate the relative probabilities of one- and two-proton emission from the compound system of $^{6}$Li + $^{51}$V through high-resolution 16-GeV/c proton-proton collisions. The relative probabilities of one-proton, two-proton, and alpha particle emission are measured as a nuclear yield increase approaches its peak. The ratio of two-proton to alpha particle emission shows a significant decrease as the yield approaches its peak. The researchers observe that above the threshold for 16-GeV/c proton-proton collisions, the relative probabilities of one-proton, two-protons, and alpha particles do not differ significantly, but all are lower than measured at lower energies near the threshold for 12-GeV/c proton-proton collisions. The findings suggest that the formation of alpha particles is largely the result of 1n-1n and 2p2p correlations that exceed the size of the alpha particle.

A novel and efficient method for an animal to move is climbing, particularly effective in scenarios where the terrain's friction resistance heavily favors ascent over descent. Many creatures, including geckos, chameleons, and lampreys, exhibit this mode of locomotion. It has been extensively studied in animals that are much larger than the size of the objects they climb on. This project investigates how the Pacific lamprey uses force to climb on a plane with varying levels of friction, and finds that its movement is largely influenced by two major factors: the interaction between its body and the environment, and the position of its body components. The analysis of the obtained data suggests that the Pacific lamprey employs a unique gait that could provide insights for the design of robotic systems that mimic its behavior.

We develop a model that simulates the colon cancer tumor microenvironment as a dynamic process governed by a Feynman-Vernon-Bird type Fokker-Planck equation, with the goal of identifying an optimal treatment strategy to maximize the immune system's effectiveness in fighting the tumor for a specific patient. The Fokman-Planck equation is derived using Itō stochastic dynamics and its coefficients are optimized through a machine learning process, utilizing patient data. Subsequently, the equation's coefficients are interpreted in a meaningful way and used to define different treatment policies, which are evaluated and compared to determine the most suitable course of action.

In IoT applications, the effectiveness of D2D communication is frequently underpinned by a generative modeling approach. However, the efficiency of the D2D system depends on the update time of the system's information, not its coverage area, which is influenced by age of information (AoI). By utilizing a deep neural network, this research aims to optimize the pairwise transmission policies to minimize the average AoI. These policies are unknown variables, requiring approximation through the utilization of a deep policy network. A neural network model based on the policy network is trained by employing a variational bound on the average AoI, resulting in a deep learning approach for D2D systems. The results show that this method converges to an efficient transmission policy that maximizes the system's spectral efficiency while ensuring it converges to a mixture of on/off modes and zero, zero, and binary modes. The latter correspond to modes where a node transmits from a packet, transmits from a fresh packet, or remains idle.

We develop a proof that helicity is preserved over time for solutions obtained using Lagrangian trajectories in a specific framework for the compressible Euler equations, particularly for fluids with zero pressure and internal energy as functions of the density. This outcome is contingent upon the assumption that the solution has a spatially bounded velocity field and that the solution itself remains spatially bounded, with its gradient also bounded. This confirms a long-standing conjecture initially proposed by Anand Mohan and S. S. Jha in 1988.

The researchers in a particular study demonstrated that for a specific type of equation, occurring in both one and two dimensions, a particular solution $u(x,t)$ has a large value in its magnitude, given certain conditions are met. This magnitude in $u(x,t)$ becomes even more pronounced as time $t$ increases. Additionally, the researchers found that for a specific ratio of coefficients in the equation, the magnitude in $u(x,t)$ behaves arbitrarily closely to any value within the interval $[-1,1]$.

Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of binary black hole systems reveal that small, non-circular orbit eccentricities persist until the point of merger. Failing to account for these residual eccentricities in predictions of gravitational-wave characteristics from these events could lead to inaccurate conclusions, particularly when analyzing a large number of events. We have developed a method to determine the residual eccentricity at merger as a function of inspiral frequency, which is further divided into two parts: one applicable to lower frequency ranges, approximately $10^{-2}-10^{-4}$ Hz, and another for higher frequency ranges. We have found that in the frequency range of $10^{-2}-10^{-4}$ Hz the eccentricity of approximately $10^{-3}-10^{-5}$ applies, while in the frequency range of $10^{-5}-10^{-7}$ Hz the eccentricity of approximately $10^{-6}-10^{-8}$ applies. We have discovered that in order to achieve an accuracy of one-half the least significant bit, a large number, approximately $10^{11}$, of gravitational-waves must be considered. In contrast, a large number, approximately $10^{16}$, of gravitational-waves must be considered in order to determine the residual eccentricity accurately. We have established that in systems with total mass and redshifted mass the split between inspiral and merger phases occurs at a frequency of approximately $10^{-3}$ Hz.

A proposed concept combines the capabilities of a free-electron laser oscillator and a free-electron laser to create a high-intensity X-ray amplifier with the potential to reach record-breaking levels of nearly terawatt power. This concept leverages the coordination of the oscillator's gain and the electron beam's feedback to achieve nearly complete amplification. To demonstrate the feasibility of this concept, detailed simulations of the oscillator's feedback dynamics and the properties of the seed X-ray pulse are conducted. The simulations' outcomes confirm that the full coherence of the X-ray pulse can persist through multiple passes in the free-electron laser amplifier, yielding a pulse with the record-breaking intensity of around 200 TW.

Detecting unusual incidents in real-time is vital for effective event monitoring, particularly in transportation systems. Current approaches using Dynamic Graphs have several limitations, such as relying on predefined rules for detection, a complex rule creation process, and difficulty in adapting to unfamiliar patterns of an event. Recent methods employing machine learning algorithms with a focus on detection are challenging to execute in real-time due to their reliance on extensive data normalization and a large training dataset of labeled nodes. In order to overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a new approach called Dynamic Graph Anomaly (DGA), which uses a time-based segmentation technique to divide the graph into equal periods and analyze the similarity of nodes within each segment to identify anomalies. DGA addresses the challenges of real-time detection, such as processing capability, label availability, and incident generalization, by incorporating thresholds for similarity calculation and optimizing its performance by testing various values. Our method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing approaches in various scenarios, with successful implementations in two real-world cases involving traffic monitoring in the United States cities of Boston and San Francisco.

The structure of an imploding shock wave in a medium with varying density has been derived using similarity solutions. The equations governing this shock wave, which forms during the collapse of a cloud in star formation, can be transformed into a dimensionless form through a change of variable. Assuming a self-similar solution exists and using standard methods of dimensionality reduction, we obtain a closed system of ordinary differential equations. However, due to the initial conditions being outside the range of validity for this self-similar solution, a two-part solution is necessary to accurately represent the shock wave's behavior across its entire life cycle. In addition, we provide an in-depth examination of the global conservation laws in this context, including the total energy and momentum of the shock wave.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly being utilized in almost every aspect of our lives, and its capabilities are being utilized by organizations of all sizes to resolve complex issues. However, its widespread adoption has also raised concerns about its lack of transparency and the unforeseen consequences of its predictions, which could lead to significant harm if AI systems are deployed without being properly evaluated. Explainability, a crucial requirement for AI systems, is the capacity of these systems to provide transparent and understandable justifications for their outputs. Despite the importance of examining this requirement, explainability is often overlooked during AI development. This paper proposes an innovative approach that enables the systematic investigation of explainability as a critical factor in the successful implementation of AI systems. By drawing parallels between requirements engineering and explainability, this approach identifies various aspects of explainability that require thorough analysis. Ultimately, this approach can serve as a foundation for creating a comprehensive framework that facilitates the identification, modeling, and fulfillment of explainability needs in AI systems.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for signs of cancer, which requires a significant amount of time and expertise. Recent advancements in deep learning technology have made it possible to automate this process, although a significant obstacle remains: the limited availability of high-quality histopathological images paired with detailed and accurate clinical annotations. In an effort to overcome this challenge, we have created UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9533 annotated images derived from 322 rectal resections, 2029 chromo-endoscopes, and 1918 virtual chromo-endoscopes. This dataset allows for the training and testing of deep learning models capable of classifying colorectal polyps into three types: high-grade dysplasia, low-grade dysplasia, and non-dysplasia. Additionally, by labeling various histological features, we have developed models for grading polyps as benign, pre-cancerous, or cancerous. Our experiments demonstrate that with the help of this new dataset, a state-of-the-art model can achieve superior performance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we have observed significant improvements in loss functions that directly quantify prediction errors.

A new aspect of zero-error source coding has been explored, where a source coder attempts to prevent part of the encoded data from being transmitted to a decoder who has access to a channel output sequence. The motivation behind this is the realization that source coding algorithms are inherently vulnerable to data leakage due to their reliance on channel output sequences as feedback. The comfort level with this scenario can vary depending on the level of privacy required. We've approached this challenge by focusing on the general case and developed complete characterizations, utilizing graph theory, to determine the minimum amount of leaked information while maintaining acceptable reconstruction quality. We've also established a new fundamental bound in this context and investigated its applicability to specific source coding problems. Ultimately, we have identified the constraints that must be satisfied for the source coder to successfully prevent data leakage while achieving satisfactory reconstruction quality.

A new non-hierarchical deep generative model, specifically designed for microwave radiation, is introduced in order to enhance quality of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images. The system consists of two layers: a feature extraction component that detects targets in SAR images, and a generative component, based on a variational autoencoder (VAE), which learns a probability distribution of the integrated features. The extraction component integrates multiple targets using a self-attention mechanism, allowing for target aggregation and contextual information consideration. The system was tested on the four classes of targets found in the MSTAR dataset and achieved AUC values of 0.976, 0.973, 0.973, and 0.969. The performance of MrSARP was compared to a comparable model, LowSARP, and a industry standard feature-based classifier, showing MrSARP to be more accurate in classification. The system was further tested on various datasets and showed its effectiveness in automatic target recognition (ATR) and image enhancement.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant incorporates variational techniques with classical optimization approaches. One method to refine its parameters involves marking them as control variables in a Bayesian sampling process. We discovered that by treating these parameters as uncertain variables and collecting associated data, we can accurately determine their mean value through Bayesian estimation. As a result, a posterior probability distribution for the solution's quality is developed. Furthermore, we found that the variance of the approximation's uncertainty distribution serves as a reliable predictor for its precision. Consequently, incorporating Bayesian concepts into QAOA leads to a reliable and precise estimate of the solution's quality, along with an accurate prediction of its uncertainty. The implementation of this technique in a real-world circuit design results in a robust and predictable solution.

This research develops a method to compute the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach calculates the intersection regions of the two ellipses by examining five distinct cases resulting from different relative orientations of the ellipses. Each case involves calculating the area of intersection between two elliptical circles. The findings are further demonstrated by visualizing the intersection regions using a graphical user interface implemented in C++.

Our research focuses on continuous-duration $q$-learning for simulations where the time horizon is not pre-defined. It's necessary to have a continuous time model to determine the duration of episodes. We developed a theoretical framework to ensure that existing methods for continuous-duration $q$-learning are consistently applicable and reliable. Furthermore, we discovered that existing algorithms require additional conditions to guarantee convergence in the absence of a pre-defined time horizon. We introduced two new types of continuous-duration reinforcement learning problems, called the "episode management problem" and the "duration management problem," and found that existing problem transformations can solve these issues. We showed that using value function approximation can solve the "episode management problem" when the duration can be predicted. We proposed a new approach, called "duration-based double q-learning," which guarantees convergence without any particular condition. We tested double q-learning using both simulated M/M/1/2 queues and the "episode management problem," demonstrating its reliability.

Quantum magnets' dynamical structure factor is a critical measurement, but making predictions for multi-dimensional models like Hubbard is complicated due to computational and theoretical constraints. We investigated magnetic excitations of the Hubbard model on a triangular lattice with longer-range hopping. Beginning with the 120-degree and striped patterns, we used density matrix decomposition to calculate the dynamical structure factor and discovered that long-range magnetic order arises from spin interactions in an inherently disordered state. We found that long-range magnetic order transitions share characteristics with those of the Heisenberg model, and that the density of states affects long-range magnetic order patterns. Our results, combined with insights from quantum Monte Carlo simulations, explain the phase diagram's anisotropy and the occurrence of long-range magnetic order at certain densities, which is a manifestation of order-by-disorder phenomenon.

This research introduces an innovative, automated approach for identifying and pinning the locations of vertebras in CT scans without requiring manual landmarl placement. The method, Vert-Loco, locates vertebrae by minimizing the distortion of spinal anatomy and matches their expected appearance from posterior-to-anterior X-ray views. Vert-Loco's optimization process is influenced by two constraints: one ensures that vertebrae are aligned in a straight line and another ensures that their positions on adjacent images are aligned. Vert-Loco demonstrates excellent performance, with mean Charbonnier error rates of 0.28 and 0.30 for L1-L2 and L2-L3, respectively, and successfully localizes all vertebrae in the majority of scans, even in those containing artificial or pathological distortions. The development of Vert-Loco's anatomy-constrained optimization process represents a significant advancement in using spine deformation constraints for vertebrae localization. Additionally, the approach's ability to locate all vertebrae, even when there are abnormalities or distortions, is an important consideration in clinical applications. Vert-Loco represents a robust, general-purpose approach for vertebrae localization and can be adapted for various spine-related tasks. The findings support the use of Vert-Loco as a reliable reference point for similar tasks and suggest that, with further modification, it can address more complex challenges. The implementation of Vert-Loco is open to use by other researchers and clinical practitioners for evaluation and adaptation.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes between quantifiable microscopic states. The flow rates of physical processes are calculated from the anti-symmetric transition measures defined on the state space and the transition space. The statistical behavior of these flow rates can be represented by normalized cumulants. The current cumulant is influenced by the jump process's memory function, which is defined by its higher-order cumulants. The average and higher-order statistics of the flow rates are independent of the choice of flux, provided the underlying microstates and transition processes are valid. The flux's unit also plays a part in the invariance. The statistical invariance suggests that the flux's distribution and its higher-order statistics remain unchanged when the flux is scaled. The condition for invariance may be satisfied by selecting an appropriate flux unit that varies based on the system's driving forces. The driving forces can be represented by a divergence-based metric that depends on the system's equilibrium characteristics.

This research extends the relative quantum field theory to any dimension, allowing for the calculation of a key physical amplitude under specified sigma-model anomalies. It forms the foundational part of a new theory known as "bivariant relative quantum field theory." Furthermore, we create a quantum field theory that remains invariant through birational transformations, similar to how nonrelativistic theories can remain invariant under Lie symmetries. When the underlying surface has a symmetry that can be represented as a BPS algebra, we show that the amplitude corresponding to the relative flat connection can be reduced to a calculation of the central charge of a related 2D relative quantum field theory. If the symmetry further simplifies to a superconformal algebra, then the amplitude reduces to a calculation of the three-point correlation functions of primary fields in a standard quantum field theory. Notably, the amplitude is unaffected by the $\mathcal{F}$ anomaly of the underlying relative quantum field theory, suggesting that it possesses a hidden property related to the $\mathcal{F}$ anomaly. Additionally, for the special case where the underlying surface has the structure of a torus, we find that the amplitude can be expressed using the relative flat connection of a related cohomological quantum field theory, and it takes the form of a holomorphic function of the modular parameter of the torus. Finally, we propose that the techniques used in this research, involving calculations of relative flat connections, can be applied not only to two-dimensional quantum field theories but also

Two piezoelectric materials placed on a metal surface can form a coupled system that transmits acoustic waves. When the distance between the materials is reduced, the coupling between them increases and affects wave transmission. Our research involved cutting a narrow gap in a pair of piezoelectric ceramics on a gold sheet using X-ray lithography and etching. We found that applying an external electric field caused total transmission of the transmitted signal at specific frequencies, which was confirmed by measurements of the transmitted power and the electric current induced between the materials. Their theoretical models also showed good agreement.

We suggest a novel approach based on resonator photonics, utilizing exciton-polariton condensates formed in microcavities, to achieve significant advancements in light manipulation and application. The dynamic interaction between the polariton and the resonator's electrical and optical responses enables sophisticated control over light, attaining impossible functionality in conventional photonic systems. The sector expects that this platform will yield revolutionary advancements in a range of technologies, including ultra-fast data processing, highly flexible satelite communications, and advanced imaging systems.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process of this debris still unknown. Analyzing grain size and sublimation rate is essential in comprehending the environment that contributes to planetary disintegration. In this study, the LBTI imagery is used to revise the parameters of the debris cloud surrounding a disintegrating exoplanet, K2-22b. By incorporating empirical models, our analysis reveals that the sedimenting particles have a size of around 0.5 to 1 micron, indicating larger particles are likely stuck together. Given its higher mass loss rate, the debris cloud surrounding K2-22b may originate from a series of gravitational encounters between the planet and the nearby exoplanet, K2-22 c. This could provide the necessary material that leads to the disintegration of the planet.

We establish a condition, based on the coherence of the Milnor fiber, that guarantees the projectivity of the critical locus of a polynomial system with isolated singularities. This condition unfolds into a criterion for detecting the singularity index of the system, which translates into a combinatorial constraint in the case of quasi-ordinary singularities. This report illustrates the implications of this condition through several examples.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform library designed for cross-industry data analysis on.NET. Developed using C#, Daany leverages the power of Excel to provide data analysis capabilities, incorporating popular algorithms from the scikit-learning Python library. Comprised of 200,000 lines of code, Daany is heavily based on the NetSpark library, offering a strong foundation for data science applications within the.NET framework. Its key features include data frames, series, and spreadsheet integration, making it well-suited for data analysis, machine learning, and optimization tasks.

This text explores the contrasting views of mathematicization and thinking in the scientific revolution through historical analysis. It focuses on Galileo's experience with the Medici affair, an ill-fated mathematical challenge, to illustrate the complexities of mathematical concepts. It then examines Kepler's use of geometric methods to understand planetary motions, but notes that these motions are not inherently geometric. To explain the success of mathematical physics, the text turns to von Neumann's theory of measurement in quantum mechanics, suggesting that mathematicization occurs naturally within the framework of modern science. The underlying message is a caution against confusing mathematical formulations with genuine physical thinking.

The standard cosmological model implies that the universe's early light radiation follows a perfect black-body distribution. However, this study reveals that as matter and radiation interact, deviations from this idealized model become statistically significant, particularly in the universe's early stages. Notably, these discrepancies, though minimal in density, have a notable impact on phase transitions and affect the standard model's prediction for the universe's ionization state, making a non-Gaussian distribution inevitable. To characterize this non-Gaussian behavior, thermal fluctuations during the era of matter- radiation equivalence are analyzed, focusing on ionized electrons and photons. Specifically, the variance and higher-order momenta of relevant variables are examined, showing that their sign and magnitude vary significantly. This non-Gaussian behavior leads to distinct differences in the probability distribution functions of important physical quantities, such as the fine structure constant and baryon-to-photon ratio, which are integral to understanding the universe's ionization state. In turn, this distinction influences the development of structure within these components. Importantly, these findings, though minor in density, hold substantial importance for understanding the universe's evolution at its earliest stages. Their implications, though detected, remain a subject of debate among scientists.

The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates computational models that can seamlessly integrate plasma physics into three-dimensional simulations. A novel approach utilizing the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model was implemented to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. Comparing this model to a comprehensive three-dimensional Particle-in-Cell simulation, we observe similar magnetic field dynamics and plasma responses. Notably, the MHD-AEPIC model effectively captured the core processes of magnetic reconnection, including island development, plasma heating, and collisionless growth rates, all within a significantly reduced computational resource expenditure.

This research paper introduces Amanuensis, an innovative collaborative tool designed to streamline systems education by automating menial tasks for both students and instructors. Amanuensis facilitates automated lab setup, student account creation, and error detection and resolution through artificial intelligence. By automating these time-consuming tasks, Amanuensis increases instructors' efficiency and frees up students from tedious work, allowing them to focus on high-level programming concepts. Built using open-source software, Amanuensis is currently in use at the University of Texas at San Antonio and is offered as a free resource for other educational institutions.
